passages.title: Judgment nears while people mock revelation
passages.tafsir:
Surah al-Anbiya' opens not with an argument but with an alarm. Ayah 1 announces that people's reckoning has drawn near — and in the same breath names their response to that announcement: heedlessness, and turning away. Ayat 2 to 6 then show what that heedlessness looks like from the inside. These people listen to freshly revealed words of their Lord as though they were entertainment (2), whisper against the Messenger ﷺ in private (3), receive a single crushing reply (4), throw four mutually contradictory labels at the Qur'an and then demand a miracle instead (5), and are finally reminded that the miracle they are asking for has never once produced faith in any nation before them (6). What holds the passage together is the distance between how near the Judgment is and how far the human heart has wandered from it.

Both of our sources open the surah by recalling how it was treasured. Ibn Kathir cites a report recorded by Al-Bukhari, in which 'Abdur-Rahman bin Yazid said that 'Abdullah said of Banu Isra'il, Al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta Ha and Al-Anbiya': "they are among the earliest and most beautiful Surahs and they are my treasure." Separately, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens its commentary by relating, on the authority of Qurtubi, that Sayyidna Abdullah Ibn Mas'ud ؓ said that four surahs — Al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta Ha and Al-Anbiya' — are among the earlier revelations which he valued a lot and kept close to his heart. That is worth holding in mind as you read what follows: this is not merely a scolding passage, it is a treasured one.

## "Drawn near" — near to whom? (ayah 1)

The verse says the reckoning **has drawn near**, in the past tense, as of something already accomplished. Two explanations appear in the sources, and they work together rather than competing.

**First, the collective reckoning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the reference is to the Day of Judgment — the time is near when people will have to give an account of their deeds — and that its approach is measured in relation to bygone ages, as the ummah of Sayyidna Muhammad Al-Mustafa ﷺ is the last of them all. We stand at the end of the line, not in the middle of it. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way — as a warning from Allah of the approach of the Hour, while people are heedless of it, meaning, in his words, that they are not working for it or preparing for it. He sets the verse beside Allah's words, "The Event ordained by Allah will come to pass, so seek not to hasten it," and "The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has been cleft asunder. And if they see a sign, they turn away" (54:1–2). That second pairing is our whole passage in miniature: an announcement of nearness, met with a shrug.

**Second, the individual reckoning.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that if the word *ḥisāb* (reckoning) is taken in its general sense, then the reckoning in the grave is included too — which each individual faces immediately after death. It is for this reason, it says, that an individual's death is regarded as his Day of Reckoning, citing the maxim *man māta faqad qāmat qiyāmatuh*: "for a person who has died, his Day of Reckoning has arrived." Read this way the verse becomes unanswerable. You may argue about how far off the Hour is. You cannot argue about how far off your own death is — as Maʿārif puts it, the individual reckoning for everyone is not very far, no matter how long one lives, because death is certain and no one knows when it will befall.

## Heedless — and where exactly? (ayah 1)

The ayah describes them as *fī ghaflatin muʿriḍūn*: sunk in heedlessness, turning away. Ibn Kathir records that An-Nasa'i transmitted from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet ﷺ, that on the words "while they turn away in heedlessness" he ﷺ said: *fī'd-dunyā* — "in this world."

Two words, and they diagnose everything. The heedlessness is not a gap in information; these people have been told. It is a location. Their attention lives somewhere — in this world — and the Hereafter is simply not where they are standing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points the warning squarely at the reader: the underlying message of the verse is to warn those people, whether believers or non-believers, who are in a state of slumber due to indulgence in worldly affairs, unmindful of the certainty that all this will come to an end one day. And then it says something bracing — that it is this disregard of the Day of Judgment which is the root cause of all ills.

## Listening while playing (ayat 2–3)

Ayah 2 sharpens the picture: no new reminder comes to them from their Lord but they listen to it *while they are playing*, and ayah 3 completes the sentence — *lāhiyatan qulūbuhum*, their hearts paying no heed.

Notice what the ayah does **not** accuse them of. It does not say they refuse to listen. It says they listen; the ears are working. The failure is one layer down, in the heart, which is elsewhere the whole time.

Ibn Kathir explains *muḥdath* — the word describing the reminder — as meaning **newly-revealed**. He frames the passage as Allah stating that they do not listen to the revelation (*waḥy*) He sends down to His Messenger ﷺ, an address, he says, to the Quraysh and all disbelievers like them. And here Ibn Kathir brings a striking remark of Ibn 'Abbas, of which he notes that Al-Bukhari recorded something similar: "Why do you ask the People of the Book about what they have, which has been altered and distorted, and they have added things and taken things away, when your Book is the most recently revealed from Allah, and you read it pure and unadulterated?" The freshness of the revelation is precisely its honour — and the people of ayah 2 treat that freshness as the day's amusement.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers three ways of reading their "playing," and each is recognisable:

- They make light of the new Qur'anic verses when these are recited before them, being totally oblivious of the fear of Allah and of the Hereafter.
- They keep themselves engaged in their own amusement and take no notice of the Qur'anic verses when these are recited before them.
- They ridicule the Qur'anic verses themselves.

The first is a failure of weight, the second of attention, the third open mockery. Maʿārif also frames ayah 2 together with the opening of ayah 3 as describing the state of those who disregard the punishment in the grave and in the Hereafter and do not prepare themselves to counter it with good deeds — which ties this description straight back to the reckoning announced in ayah 1.

## The whispering (ayah 3)

The ayah then turns to what they say when they think no one is listening: "Those who do wrong conceal their private counsels" — Ibn Kathir explains *najwā* here as what they say to one another in secret. Two things are whispered.

**"Is this more than a human being like you?"** Ibn Kathir says this refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: they did not believe he could be a Prophet because he was a human being like them — how, they reasoned, could he alone be singled out to receive revelation, and not them? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same objection in their own terms: they used to discuss among themselves secretly that his claim to prophethood should not be accepted, because he was an ordinary human being like all others and not an angel.

**"Will you then submit to magic, while you see it?"** Ibn Kathir gives the sense: will you follow him and be like one who submits to magic when he knows that it is magic? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what drove them to this particular slander, and it is one of the most illuminating notes in the whole passage. Not even the most rigid among the unbelievers could deny the supreme charm and eloquence of the Book of Allah, nor its power to influence people when it was recited before them. They could not argue with the effect. So, in order to turn people away from it, they attached a name to the effect: magic, black art. They thought that labelling the Qur'an a book of magic would keep people away from Islam, dissuading them from going to the Holy Prophet ﷺ and listening to the Qur'an.

And why in secret? Maʿārif suggests they probably discussed the subject secretly among themselves lest the Muslims come to know about their foolish views and unveil their fallacy. That is the tell. An argument confident of itself does not need to be whispered.

## One sentence in reply (ayah 4)

To all of that — the whispering, the labels, the strategy — comes a single answer: "My Lord knows what is said in the heavens and on earth. And He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower." The translation renders this as the Prophet's ﷺ own response; Ibn Kathir introduces it as what Allah said in response to their fabrications and lies.

There is no counter-argument, no defence of his character ﷺ. There is only the naming of the One who was in the room. Ibn Kathir draws out both edges of it.

**Nothing at all is hidden from Him.** Ibn Kathir's words are exactly that: nothing at all is hidden from the One Who knows what is said in the heavens and on earth. Those closed-door counsels, then, were never private. And of "He is the All-Hearer, the All-Knower" he says that He hears all that they say and knows all their circumstances — and he calls this a warning and a threat to them.

**And therefore the Qur'an could only be from Him.** This is the quiet second blow. Ibn Kathir points out that the One who knows all of that is the very One who reveals this Qur'an — a Book which contains news of the earliest and last generations. No one can produce the like of it except the One who knows all the secrets of the heavens and the earth. So the reply to "he invented it" is already contained in the reply to "we said it in private."

## Four labels that cancel one another (ayah 5)

Ayah 5 reports their verdicts, each introduced by *bal* — "no, rather" — as though they keep retracting and trying again. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the sequence: in the first place the unbelievers called the Qur'an magic; then they described it as a collection of disturbed dreams; then they said it was a forgery and fabrication against Allah to call it His words; and finally they said that he ﷺ was a poet and the Qur'an represented his poetic compositions.

On *aḍghāth aḥlām*, Maʿārif explains that dreams having an element of personal and shaitanic thoughts are called *aḍghāth aḥlām* — which is why the phrase is rendered "hotch-potch dreams": a jumble, not a true vision.

Look at the four together and they destroy one another. Magic is deliberate craft; jumbled dreams are involuntary confusion. Fabrication is conscious lying; poetry is inspired art. A man cannot be at once a sorcerer, a dreamer, a forger and a poet. Ibn Kathir reads exactly this into the passage: it tells us of the stubbornness of the disbelievers, the various things they said about the Qur'an, and how confused and misguided they were about it — sometimes describing it as magic, sometimes as poetry, or mixed up false dreams, or a fabrication. He cites Allah's words: "See what examples they have put forward for you. So they have gone astray, and never can they find a way" (17:48). People who have found the truth agree on what it is. People running from it need a new label every week.

## "Then let him bring us a sign" (ayat 5–6)

Their labels exhausted, they change the subject to a demand: let him bring us a sign like the ones that were sent before. Ibn Kathir says they were referring to the she-camel of Salih and the signs of Musa and 'Isa. Maʿārif adds that they were demanding certain specific miracles as proof of his being a real Prophet.

The reply in ayah 6 is not a refusal but a piece of history: "Not one of the towns which We destroyed before them believed — will they then believe?" Ibn Kathir spells out the pattern: none of the peoples to whom Messengers were sent were given a sign at the hands of their Prophet and believed; on the contrary they disbelieved, and were destroyed as a result. Would these people believe in a sign if they saw it? Not at all. He cites: "Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment" (10:96–97). And on the withholding of the demanded signs he cites, "And nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them" (17:59).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this a step further, and turns what looks like a denial into a mercy. The same demand for miracles was made by peoples in the past from their prophets, and when their request was met it was of no avail — they did not submit to Allah even after witnessing the miracles of their choice. And Allah has decreed that people who do not submit to Him even after seeing the miracle of their choice are subjected to His wrath even in this world and are destroyed. But in His Divine Mercy, and in view of the honoured position of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, Allah had granted his ummah immunity from that terrible punishment which is the inevitable fate of those who defy the Will of Allah. It was therefore not considered desirable to show them miracles of their choice — because if they, like the earlier people, persisted in their unbelief even after seeing those miracles, they too would invite the wrath of Allah. And Maʿārif reads the closing question of ayah 6, "Will they believe?", as a hint that there was no likelihood of these people accepting the true faith even after seeing the miracles of their choice; hence they were not shown the desired miracle. The sign was withheld not to starve them of proof but to spare them the fate that would have followed.

For proof they had in abundance. Ibn Kathir insists that they witnessed clear signs and definitive proof at the hands of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — signs, he says, far clearer and more overwhelming than any that had been witnessed in the case of any other Prophet, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all. The problem was never a shortage of evidence.

## What the passage asks of us

**Take the announcement personally.** Maʿārif is explicit that ayah 1 warns believers as much as non-believers — anyone asleep in worldly preoccupation. And on the reading that includes the reckoning of the grave, "drawn near" is not a statement about world history; it is a statement about you.

**Measure heedlessness by preparation, not by belief.** Ibn Kathir defines being heedless of the Hour as not working for it and not preparing for it. A person can hold the Day of Judgment to be certain and still be described by ayah 1, if nothing in his week is actually being done for it.

**Audit how you listen.** Ayah 2 convicts people whose ears are open and whose hearts are elsewhere. Maʿārif's three readings — making light of a verse, half-hearing it while busy with amusement, or mocking it — make a usable checklist for the next time Qur'an is recited in your hearing.

**Value what is in your hands.** Ibn 'Abbas's question is aimed at us as much as at those he addressed: you hold the most recently revealed Book from Allah, and you read it pure and unadulterated. Ayah 2 is about people who had that in front of them and played through it.

**Stop waiting for one more sign.** Ayah 6 closes off the excuse that a bigger miracle would settle matters. The nations who were given their miracle did not believe. Faith was never waiting on evidence; it was waiting on the heart in ayah 3 to come back into the room.

passages.title: Messengers were only mortal men
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath:** the deniers had objected that a prophet ought to be something more than an ordinary man — so Allah answers that every messenger before Muhammad ﷺ was exactly this: a human being who ate food, walked in the markets, and eventually died, but who carried revelation. What holds ayat 7–10 together is a single chain of reasoning: the messengers were men (7), with ordinary bodies and ordinary lifespans (8), yet Allah's promise through them was fulfilled and the evildoers were destroyed (9), and now that same revelation has come to *you* — and it is not a humiliation but an honour (10).

## The objection Allah is answering

Ibn Kathir opens his comment plainly: "Here Allah refutes those who denied that human Messengers could be sent." The objection was not academic. It was the sneer of people who looked at the Messenger ﷺ living an unremarkable daily life and concluded that greatness could not possibly look like that.

Ibn Kathir reports what the earlier nations said when they denied this: **"Shall mere men guide us?"** (64:6) — the flat refusal that a human being could be a source of guidance. Hear what is inside that question. It is not a request for evidence. It is an objection to *status*: a messenger who lived among them was too close, too available, too much like them to be obeyed.

## Ayah 7: "only men to whom We revealed"

Allah's reply in ayah 7 is a categorical statement about all of sacred history: *We did not send before you except men to whom We sent revelation.* Ibn Kathir spells out the force of it — "all the Messengers who came before you were men, human beings. There were no angels among them." Not one exception in the entire record.

He supports it with two further verses. From Surah Yusuf: "And We sent not before you any but men unto whom We revealed, **from among the people of townships**" (12:109) — not merely human, but local, drawn from settled communities, people with neighbours and names. And Surah al-Ahqaf: "Say: 'I am not a new thing among the Messengers...'" (46:9) — the Prophet ﷺ is not an innovation, not an oddity. He stands in a long, consistent line.

Notice the one thing the ayah *does* single out about them: **nūḥī ilayhim** — "to whom We send revelation." Everything else about them was ordinary. That clause is the whole of their distinction, and the passage will return to it in ayah 8.

Ibn Kathir then draws out the mercy hidden inside the objection: "This is a part of the perfect blessing of Allah towards His creation: He sent to them Messengers from among themselves so that they could receive the Message from them and learn from them." The very thing the deniers held against the Messenger ﷺ — that he was one of them — is the thing that made the message learnable. You cannot take a pattern of life from an angel. You can take it from a man who prays, eats, trades, grieves and endures in front of you.

## "So ask the people of the Reminder"

The second half of ayah 7 turns the argument over to the disbelievers' own resources: **fas'alū ahl al-dhikr in kuntum lā taʿlamūn** — "So ask the people of the Reminder, if you do not know."

Ibn Kathir explains the intent: ask the people of knowledge among the nations, "such as the Jews and Christians and other groups" — put the question to them: *were the Messengers who came to you human beings or angels?* And the answer, he says, comes back unavoidably: "Indeed they were human beings." It is an argument the deniers could not wriggle out of, because it did not rest on the testimony of the believers at all. It rested on the memory of the communities who had received prophets before them.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** examines the phrase *ahl al-dhikr* itself. It notes that in this verse the scholars of the Injīl (Gospel) and the Torah are referred to as *ahl al-dhikr* — those among them who had accepted the prophethood of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. The sense, it says, is: "if you are not aware whether the prophets of the past were angels or ordinary men then you should find out from the scholars of Injil and Torah as they know perfectly well that all prophets were human beings." It then adds a wider possibility — that the term may refer to all Jews and Christians, even those who had not believed in the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ. On this reading the argument is stronger still, because a hostile witness who confirms your point is the most persuasive witness there is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents this second sense as "quite possible," so it is fair to hold both readings rather than force one.

**A ruling drawn from the verse.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Qurtubi has said in his exegesis that this verse has made it clear that ignorant persons who are not acquainted with the rules of the Sharīʿah must seek knowledge from scholars and then follow them accordingly. This is one of the great practical yields of ayah 7. The verse's original context is a specific historical question, but the principle it plants is permanent: **when you do not know, ask someone who does.** Islam does not ask every believer to become a jurist; it asks every believer to stop guessing. The condition attached — *in kuntum lā taʿlamūn*, "if you do not know" — is honest about the human tendency to bluff. The cure for not knowing is not confidence. It is a question.

## Ayah 8: bodies that ate, lives that ended

Ayah 8 removes the last two props from the objection. *We did not make them bodies that ate no food, nor were they immortal.*

**They ate.** Ibn Kathir: "rather they had bodies that ate food," and he cites al-Furqan: "And We never sent before you any of the Messengers but verily, they ate food and walked in the markets" (25:20). Then comes the line worth sitting with. Those messengers, he writes, "were human beings who ate and drank like all other people, and they went to the marketplaces to earn a living and engage in business; **that did not affect them adversely or reduce their status in any way**, as the idolators imagined."

That last clause is the correction of a whole way of seeing. The deniers assumed that ordinary human need — hunger, work, the marketplace — was beneath prophethood; that a real man of Allah would float above the economy. The Qur'an says the opposite: earning a living took nothing away from them. Nobility in Islam is not detachment from ordinary life. It is what a person carries *through* ordinary life.

Ibn Kathir then quotes the objectors in their own words: **And they say: "Why does this Messenger eat food, and walk about in the markets. Why is not an angel sent down to him to be a warner with him? Or (why) has not a treasure been granted to him, or why has he not a garden whereof he may eat?"** (25:7–8). That is the demand laid bare: an angelic escort, sudden wealth, a private garden. Spectacle, not proof.

**They died.** "Nor were they immortals" — Ibn Kathir glosses: not immortal "in this world; on the contrary, they lived, then they died." He brings a verse from later in this very surah: "And We granted not to any human being immortality before you" (21:34). No prophet was exempt from the grave. Whatever veneration the messengers deserve, it never crosses into imagining them as something other than creatures — mortal, dependent, sustained by Allah like everyone else. This is the hinge on which sound belief about the prophets turns: honour them completely, and never lift them out of the category of created human beings.

**So what did set them apart?** Ibn Kathir answers directly: "what distinguished them from others was that they received revelation from Allah, and the angels brought down to them from Allah His rulings concerning His creation, what He commanded and what He prohibited." Not a different biology. Not exemption from death. A different *relationship*: Allah spoke, and they were the ones entrusted to carry what He said.

## Ayah 9: the promise that came true

Having established what the messengers were, ayah 9 tells you what happened. *Then We fulfilled to them the promise: We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed al-Musrifīn.*

Ibn Kathir identifies the promise precisely: it was "the promise that their Lord made to destroy the evildoers. Allah fulfilled His promise and did that."

Notice how the ayah sorts humanity into three, and how tightly:

1. **The messengers** — saved. Every long season in which a messenger seemed to be losing ended with Allah proving true to what He had said to him.
2. **"And whom We willed"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as "their followers among the believers." Deliverance extended past the prophet to the ordinary people who believed him when believing him was costly. And note the wording Allah chose: *wa man nashāʾ*, "and whom We willed" — the outcome stays anchored in Allah's will, not in anyone's claim upon Him.
3. **Al-Musrifīn** — destroyed. Ibn Kathir defines them here by their essential act: "those who disbelieved the Message brought by the Messengers."

## Ayah 10: "a Book in which is your dhikr"

The passage ends by turning from history to the reader: *Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your dhikr — will you not then use reason?*

Ibn Kathir says that here Allah "points out the noble status of the Qur'an and urges them to recognize its worth." And on the word *dhikrukum* he transmits the comment of **Ibn ʿAbbās**: "**Honor for you.**"

That single gloss reverses the entire complaint. The deniers had treated revelation through an ordinary man as something demeaning, a message not grand enough for them. Allah tells them it is their *honour* — arriving in their own language through one of their own. Ibn Kathir pairs it with al-Zukhruf: "And verily, this is indeed a Reminder for you and your people, **and you will be questioned**" (43:44). Honour and accountability come in the same package. To be handed the Qur'an is to be raised — and to be answerable for what you did with the elevation.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** develops this under the heading *The Holy Qur'an is an honour and pride for the Arabs*: the word *dhikr* here is used for "honour, excellence and fame," so the revelation of the Qur'an in the Arabic language is "a great honour and everlasting fame for the Arabs and they should value it as such." It then makes a historical observation: by Allah's mercy and by the blessings of the Qur'an the Arabs dominated the world and ruled over it for a long time — and this was "not because of any tribal or linguistic supremacy but because of Qur'an." Its blunt conclusion: "If there was no Qur'an, probably no one would have known about the Arabs at all."

That is a lesson about far more than one nation. Whatever standing a people gain through this Book is borrowed from the Book, never owned by them. Set the Qur'an aside and the honour goes with it.

Then the closing challenge: **afalā taʿqilūn** — "will you not then use reason?" Ibn Kathir reads it as: "will you not understand this blessing, and accept it?" It is striking that the passage which began by answering an objection ends not with a threat but with an appeal to the mind. Recognising the value of what you have been given is treated here as an act of basic intelligence.

## Living it

**Stop demanding that guidance look impressive.** The objectors of 25:7–8 wanted an angel, a treasure, a garden. What they were given was a man who ate food and walked in the markets, carrying the truth. Truth still tends to arrive in unglamorous packaging, and the instinct that dismisses it — *this is too ordinary to be important* — is exactly the instinct ayat 7–8 were sent to correct.

**Ask.** Qurtubi's ruling, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits it, turns ayah 7 into a daily discipline: when you do not know a matter of the religion, take it to those who do, and act on what they tell you. Not knowing is not a fault. Guessing is.

**Love the messengers without divinising them.** Ayah 8 is the guardrail. They ate; they died; they were created, sustained human beings. Their distinction was revelation, not immunity from being human.

**Let the market not diminish you.** They "went to the marketplaces to earn a living and engage in business; that did not affect them adversely or reduce their status in any way." A believer's ordinary working life is not a lesser compartment of their religion.

**Treat the Qur'an as your honour.** Ibn ʿAbbās's one-line comment — *honour for you* — is worth carrying into every session with the Book. The question of ayah 10 is left open on purpose, and it is asked of the reader as much as of the first listeners: *afalā taʿqilūn* — will you not understand what you are holding?

passages.title: Ruined towns fleeing their own doom
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat form one continuous scene: a town that had gone on wronging itself, the moment its people finally felt the punishment coming, their panicked run, a voice mocking them back towards the comforts they had trusted, their confession, and then silence. The Qur'an does not argue here; it shows. It walks the listener through the last hour of people exactly like him.

## Ayah 11: "How many" — the sheer number of ruins

*"How many a town given to wrongdoing have We destroyed, and raised up after them another people."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss on **"how many"** is blunt: **"meaning, they were very many."** This is not one cautionary tale. The earth is littered with such places. He brings two sister ayat to make the point land: *"And how many generations have We destroyed after Nuh!"* (17:17), and *"And many a township did We destroy while they were given to wrongdoing, so that it lie in ruins"* (22:45).

Notice how the town is described — *kānat ẓālimah*, rendered by Ibn Kathir as **"given to wrongdoing"**: not one lapse but a settled character, what the place had become. And notice that it is the town that is said to be destroyed, though of course it is its people who wronged and who perished; a whole civilisation is summed up in the name of the place that housed it.

Then the second half, easy to read past: *"and raised up after them another people"* — Ibn Kathir: **"another nation which came after them."** The destruction of a wrongdoing people is not the end of the human story. History does not stop; it changes tenants. Those who thought themselves indispensable are replaced, and the replacements inherit the same test. There is a thought here worth sitting with: every one of us is among the "other peoples" raised up after somebody else's ruins.

## Ayah 12: the moment they *felt* it

*"Then, when they sensed Our torment, behold, they fled from it."*

Ibn Kathir explains the moment precisely: **"when they realized that the torment would undoubtedly come upon them, just as their Prophet had warned them."**

That last clause is the whole tragedy. Nothing new was revealed to them at that instant. The information had been in their hands the entire time; a prophet had told them exactly this. What changed was not their knowledge but their certainty — and by then the torment was already upon them.

And what does that certainty produce? *"Behold, they tried to flee from it."* Ibn Kathir: **"they tried to run away."** The word *"behold"* catches the suddenness of it: the picture snaps into view, and there they are, running.

Read the flight for what it is. Faced with the punishment of Allah, they do not turn back to Him, they do not repent, they do not call on Him — they run. Their instinct is escape, not return. And as the next ayah will make plain, the running got them nowhere.

## Ayah 13: the cruellest invitation

*"Do not flee, but return to that wherein you lived a luxurious life, and to your homes, in order that you may be questioned."*

This sounds at first like advice. It is not. Ibn Kathir is explicit: **"This is a way of ridiculing them. It will be said to them by way of ridicule: 'Do not run away from the coming torment; go back to the delights and luxuries and fine homes in which you were living.'"** He records that Qatādah said simply, **"Mocking them."**

Feel the sting of it. *Mā utriftum fīh* — the luxury they had been given, the soft living Ibn Kathir renders as "the delights and luxuries." *Wa masākinikum* — "and your homes," the solid, comfortable houses that had felt like security itself. Every one of those things had been an argument, in their minds, that they were doing fine and needed no prophet. Now those very things are named back to them: *go on then, return to them. Let them save you.* Whatever a person makes his refuge instead of Allah can one day be recited back to him as a taunt.

Then: *laʿallakum tusʼalūn* — **"in order that you may be questioned."** Ibn Kathir explains: questioned **"about whether you gave thanks for what you had."** So the ease was never simply theirs. Everything handed to a person is a gift with an account attached: wealth, houses, comfort. The question at the end is not *how much did you have*, but *what did you do with it, and did you thank the One who gave it.*

## Ayah 14: the confession that comes too late

*"They cried: 'Woe to us! Certainly we have been wrongdoers.'"*

At last they say the true thing. The very word used of their town in ayah 11 — *ẓālimah*, wrongdoing — is now on their own tongues: *innā kunnā ẓālimīn*. They are not arguing any more. They are not blaming the prophet, or fate, or each other. They admit it exactly as it was.

And Ibn Kathir's comment is one of the most sobering lines in this section: **"They will confess their sins when it will be of no benefit to them."**

That is the warning. Confession is precious inside the window in which it can still change something — while there is a life left to alter. Once the torment is *sensed*, the same words that would have counted for them earlier bring them no benefit. *Yā waylanā*, "woe to us," is the cry of someone who finally sees clearly and has nothing left to do with the seeing.

## Ayah 15: harvested, and put out

*"And that cry of theirs ceased not, till We made them as a field that is reaped, extinct."*

*Fa-mā zālat tilka daʿwāhum* — that cry went on and on. Ibn Kathir: **"they will keep on saying that, admitting their wrongdoing, until We harvest them as it were, and their movements and voices come to a stop."** Picture it: the repeated wailing of "woe to us, we were wrongdoers" as the only sound in the town, over and over, until it is cut off.

Two images end the passage, and they are chosen with care.

**Ḥaṣīd — "a field that is reaped."** Standing crops look permanent, ordered, prosperous; then in one sweep the reaper lays them flat. That is what happens to them: a whole standing population goes down together. Ibn Kathir keeps the metaphor alive in his own words — *until We harvest them, as it were*.

**Khāmidīn — "extinct."** The town had blazed with life, noise, the bustle of its luxuries — and now nothing, not a flicker, not a sound. Ibn Kathir catches both halves in one phrase: **"their movements and voices come to a stop."** Movement gone, voice gone. In ayah 12 they were running; in ayah 14 they were crying out. Now neither. The passage ends in silence, which is exactly how such places are found by whoever comes after.

## Which town was it?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some exegetes took these settlements to be **Ḥaḍūrāʼ (حضُوراء) and Qilābah (قلابہ) of Yemen**. Allah had sent a prophet there, though the reports on his name differ: some say Mūsā ibn Mīshā, others say Shuʿayb — in which case, the commentary notes, he was a different prophet from the one who lived in Madyan. According to these accounts the people killed their prophet and were, as a punishment, annihilated by the disbelieving king Nabucad Nazzar; the commentary adds that this king was placed in authority over them just as he was used as an instrument for the punishment of the Children of Israel when they strayed from the righteous path in Palestine.

Having reported all that, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives its own verdict: **"In fact, Qur'an has not identified any specific settlement. Hence it will be apt to leave the subject open, so that these settlements of Yemen may also come in its ambit."** And it seals the point the way scholars do with reports they cannot verify: *only Allah knows best.*

There is a lesson there in how to read the Qur'an. Where Allah leaves a name out, the omission is worth respecting rather than filling in. Ayah 11 says *how many* a town — the emphasis falls on the pattern, on how often this has happened, not on a single historical curiosity to be filed under one date and one place. Leaving it open lets the Yemeni settlements in, and every other such town too.

## Living it

**Do not wait to be certain.** Their downfall was not ignorance — the prophet had warned them of exactly this, as Ibn Kathir points out. It was postponement. Everything they finally admitted in ayah 14 they could have admitted while it still counted for them.

**Watch what comfort does.** The luxuries in ayah 13 are not condemned because ease is evil, but because they had become the thing these people trusted and the thing that made them deaf. The test is simple: if my income, my home, my ease were named back to me tomorrow, could I still say I was grateful, and that they never came between me and my Lord?

**Take the questioning seriously now.** Ibn Kathir says the questioning is about whether you gave thanks for what you had. That is a question you can begin answering today, at the cost of nothing but attention.

**Remember that history changes tenants.** "And raised up after them another people." No people is permanent, and no people is indispensable. The ruins in ayah 11 were once somebody's confident, comfortable, thriving town.

passages.title: Creation is not idle play
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer one question: is this universe a serious thing? Allah denies that the heavens, the earth and everything between them were made for play (ayah 16); He raises and cancels the very idea that He might have taken an amusement (ayah 17); He declares that He hurls truth at falsehood until falsehood is gone, and warns those who invent claims about Him (ayah 18); and He turns to those who are near Him — the angels — whose worship never stops (ayat 19–20).

The thread running through the whole passage is **purpose**. Creation has one. The accusations people throw at Allah have none. And the servants nearest to Allah spend themselves, night and day, in worship.

## Where the passage comes from

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the link with what came just before. The preceding ayat mention the annihilation of certain settlements. Ayah 16 then carries a suggestion: just as the creation of the earth and the sky and all other created things was according to a set design, the destruction of those settlements was also the result of a definite purpose. Neither the building nor the breaking is arbitrary.

And there is a rebuke folded inside it. Having witnessed the marvels and wonders of creation, so abundantly spread all over, manifesting Allah's omnipotence and omniscience — do they still think that all these things are futile and without significance?

## "Not as players" — the word lāʿibīn

The ayah does not say Allah did not create; it says He did not create **as players**. The denial is aimed at the *manner*, at the posture of the Creator toward His work.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two Arabic words that English blurs together:

- **laʿib** (play), from which **lāʿibīn** in ayah 16 comes, means having **no useful objective**. Maʿārif attributes this definition to the lexicographer Rāghib.
- **lahw** (pastime), the word used in ayah 17, means an act which has **no purpose at all** except to provide amusement in free time. (Maʿārif gives this gloss without naming a source for it.)

So the two ayat close two different doors. Ayah 16 denies that the universe is an exercise with no useful objective. Ayah 17 denies that Allah ever took a pastime to begin with.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the underlying attitude it is answering. The disbelievers who argue against the Holy Prophet ﷺ and the Holy Qur'an, who reject the Oneness of Allah and deny His power despite its abundant manifestations — it is apparent that they have a notion that all this creation is meant for amusement and pastime. The verse rejects that false view: a little reflection will show that even the minutest particle of the universe has its utility, and each and everything created by Allah has a purpose which speaks by itself for His omniscience and Oneness.

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 16 alongside its sister ayat. Allah created the heavens and the earth **in truth**, that is, *with justice* — as He says elsewhere, "that He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done, and reward those who do good, with what is best" (53:31). He did not create all that in vain or for mere play, and in Sūrah Ṣād: "And We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose! **That is the consideration of those who disbelieve!** Then woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire!" (38:27). Note what that ayah does: it assigns the idea of a purposeless creation to those who disbelieve, and attaches a warning to it.

## Ayah 17: the hypothetical that is withdrawn as it is spoken

*"Had We intended to have a pastime, We would have had it from Our own, if We were to do so."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in the Arabic language the word **law** ("had it been that…") is used for imaginary and non-existent things, and it is used in that sense here. The argument runs: if We were to create something for amusement, there was no need to create the earth and the sky — We could have done so from the things around Us. And Maʿārif adds the common-sense edge: even a person of ordinary common sense would not indulge in a project which has no serious purpose, to say nothing of Allah Taʿālā, who is Supreme and Exalted.

**"From Us" — min ladunnā.** Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Mujāhid that this means "From Ourself," and Mujāhid explained the sense: "**We would not have created Paradise or Hell or death or the resurrection or the Reckoning.**" That is a striking way to read it. Look at what actually exists — a Garden, a Fire, death, a raising, an accounting. If, as Maʿārif says, no sensible person launches a project with no serious purpose, then the very furniture of this universe is the furniture of seriousness.

**"If We were going to do that" — in kunnā fāʿilīn.** Ibn Kathir reports that Qatādah, as-Suddī, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī and Mughīrah bin Miqsam all understood this as: *"We will not do that."* Mujāhid said that every time the word **in** ("if") is used in the Qur'an, it is a negation. So the sentence turns on itself: the hypothetical is raised and cancelled in the same breath.

**A second reading of lahw.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the commonly accepted meaning of *lahw* is a purposeless pastime, and that this is the meaning adopted in its own translation. According to some commentators, however, the word *lahw* is also used sometimes for wife or children. On that reading, ayah 17 would be a denial of the belief of those Jews and Christians who thought that Sayyidnā ʿUzair and Sayyidnā al-Masīḥ (peace be upon them) were sons of Allah: if Allah wished to have children, why should they be from humans and not from other creatures around Him? Maʿārif closes this with *Allah knows best*, and this tafsir does the same: the first meaning is the commonly accepted one; the second is a possibility some commentators raised.

## Ayah 18: truth hurled, falsehood struck on the head

*"Instead, We launch the truth against the falsehood, which smashes it, and in no time it is nothing. And woe to you for that which you ascribe."*

The ayah opens with **bal** — rendered "Nay" and "Instead" — a hard pivot away from the notion just refuted. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the three key words:

- **qadhf** — the literal meaning is to throw horizontally; hence "launch", "hurl". It is the verb of a projectile, not of a gentle placing.
- **yadmagh** — to hit on the head, to smash it. A single decisive blow, not a long wrestling match.
- **zāhiq** — something which is gone, or vanishes without leaving a trace.

And yet the weapon is not violence. Ibn Kathir explains "We fling the truth against the falsehood" as: *'We explain the truth and thus defeat falsehood.'* The missile is exposition. Falsehood is not argued into a draw; it is explained away. Ibn Kathir's comment on the outcome is quietly vivid — "it is fading and vanishing."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties this back to ayah 16 and completes the passage's logic: Allah has not created this marvellous universe with earth and the sky for amusement; this creation is the result of a carefully thought out plan which aims at **distinguishing right from wrong**. Observation of the creations of nature leads people along the righteous path and protects them from evil — that is the idea conveyed by saying that virtue is hurled against evil and smashes its head so completely that it disappears without a trace.

**"And woe to you for that which you ascribe."** Ibn Kathir is precise about who is addressed: *O you who say that Allah has offspring* — and "that which you ascribe" means "that which you say and fabricate." The sin named here is a sin of speech and of the imagination: describing Allah as He is not.

## Ayat 19–20: the angels as evidence

Having refuted the charge, Allah now presents witnesses. Ibn Kathir titles this section simply: *Everything belongs to Allah and serves Him.* He notes that after the warning of ayah 18, Allah informs us of the servitude of the angels and how they persevere in worship night and day.

**"To Him belongs whosoever is in the heavens and on earth."** Ownership first. Every being in either realm is owned.

**"And those who are near Him"** — Ibn Kathir: *i.e., the angels.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them the same way: Allah's servants who are with Him, that is, the angels, who pray to Him all the time without ceasing. Nearness and servanthood sit together in the same phrase. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel ayah: "Al-Masīḥ will never be proud to reject being a servant of Allah, nor the angels who are the near. And whosoever rejects His worship and is proud, then He will gather them all together unto Himself" (4:172). That ayah places al-Masīḥ and the near angels side by side, and says of both that they are not too proud to be servants of Allah.

Then two things are denied of the angels, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows why exactly these two.

It is human nature, Maʿārif observes, to judge others by applying one's own situation to them. So there are two possibilities that would prevent a person from worshipping ceaselessly:

1. **Pride** — he regards it below his dignity to bow down before anyone, and therefore does not pray to Allah Taʿālā.
2. **Physical limitation** — it is physically not possible for a man to worship without a break, because he needs to rest in between.

Ayah 19 removes both. **Lā yastakbirūna ʿan ʿibādatih** — Ibn Kathir: "they do not feel proud and do not refuse to worship Him." **Wa lā yastaḥsirūn** — Ibn Kathir: "they do not get tired or feel bored." As Maʿārif puts it, the angels are free from these two constraints: they do not regard it below their dignity to worship Allah constantly, nor do they get tired or need any rest or sleep.

Ayah 20 completes it: **"They glorify His praises night and day, they never slacken"** — or, in Maʿārif's rendering, *"They proclaim His purity night and day, never slackening."* That is *tasbīḥ*: proclaiming Allah's purity. And it stands opposite the fabrications condemned in ayah 18. Where the deniers *ascribe* to Allah what they say and fabricate, the angels *proclaim His purity*.

Ibn Kathir: "They persist in their worship night and day, obeying Allah to the utmost, **and they are able to do this**," and he cites: "who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded" (66:6).

**A question, and an answer worth keeping.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Sayyidnā ʿAbdullah Ibn Ḥārith (may Allah be pleased with him) asked Kaʿb al-Aḥbār (may Allah be pleased with him) how it was that the angels kept reciting *tasbīḥ* all the time — did they not have anything else to do? And if they did, how could they do both things at once? Kaʿb replied: **"O my nephew! Does performance of any of your jobs prevent you from breathing?"** The truth, Maʿārif says, is that tasbīḥ comes to the angels just as breathing comes to human beings, continuing without stopping whatever else is being done. (Maʿārif cites this from Qurṭubī and Al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ. It is a report from an early authority, not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ.)

And Maʿārif draws the conclusion the passage is aiming at: since Allah's servants who are with Him pray to Him all the time without ceasing, **if human beings do not pray to Him it will not make any difference to Him — but they themselves will be the losers.**

## Living it

**Your life is not play either.** If the sky and the earth were not created for play, then neither were you. Whenever life starts to feel like an accident with no destination, ayah 16 is the correction.

**Notice things.** Maʿārif's argument is not abstract: a little reflection will show that even the minutest particle of the universe has its utility. Paying attention to the created order is itself the path Maʿārif describes at ayah 18 — observation of the creations of nature leading a person along the righteous path and protecting him from evil.

**Defeat falsehood by explaining truth.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 18 is a whole method: "We explain the truth and thus defeat falsehood." The Qur'an's image is forceful — something launched, striking the head of falsehood — but the weapon is clarity. That should make a believer patient and precise rather than loud.

**Watch what you say about Allah.** "Woe to you for that which you ascribe" is, in Ibn Kathir's gloss, a warning about "that which you say and fabricate." Speak about Allah only with what He and His Messenger ﷺ have said about Him — affirming what He affirmed of Himself, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying His words of their meaning.

**Worship is not a favour you do Allah.** Maʿārif states it plainly: if we do not pray to Him it makes no difference to Him; we ourselves are the losers. He already has servants who never slacken, night or day.

**Aim for breathing, not sprinting.** Kaʿb's answer reframes what continuous worship even means. You are not being asked to abandon your work. You are being invited toward a life in which remembrance runs underneath the work the way breath runs underneath everything you do — quiet, constant, never stopping.

passages.title: No gods besides Allah in existence
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat form one sustained case against idolatry — a case argued rather than merely asserted. Allah does not simply forbid worshipping others; He puts the claim of the idolaters on trial and takes it apart: first by testing what their gods can actually do, then by showing that a shared sovereignty could not hold the universe together, and finally by demanding evidence and setting against it the unbroken testimony of every revealed Book and every messenger. Running underneath the whole passage is a single demand: **if you claim there is another god, show cause.**

## An audit of capability

The passage opens with a question that is really an exposure: *"Or have they taken gods from the earth, who can raise the dead?"*

Two things in that question carry the sting. The first is **"from the earth."** As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah is showing "how foolish and ignorant the polytheists are that they have made their gods from amongst the creatures of the earth." The gods being defended are themselves creatures — part of the very order that needs a Maker.

The second is the test Allah applies: **"who can raise the dead."** Ibn Kathir gives the sense — "can they bring the dead back to life and bring them forth from the earth?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the plain fact about these earth-gods: they "do not have the power of life and death," and draws the conclusion that governs the whole passage — only a Being who has these powers is worthy of being worshipped.

So the question answers itself. Ibn Kathir: "They cannot do any of that, so how can they make them rivals to Allah and worship them alongside Him?" Notice the shape of the argument. It does not begin in abstract theology; it begins with an audit of capability. Worship is owed to the One who gives life and raises the dead. Whatever cannot do that has no claim on a heart.

## One sovereign, or none at all

Having shown that the rivals cannot *do* anything, the passage moves to show that they could not even *exist*: *"Had there been other gods besides Allah in the heavens or the earth, both would have been ruined."*

Ibn Kathir reads "therein" as "in the heavens and the earth," and sets beside it the parallel from Sūrah al-Muʼminūn: *"No son did Allah beget, nor is there any god along with Him. Then each god would have taken away what he had created, and some would have tried to overcome others! Glorified be Allah above all that they attribute to Him!"* (23:91). Multiple gods would mean partition and then rivalry — each carrying off his own creation, each pushing against the others.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the logic step by step.** It calls this "an argument of common nature in favour of the Oneness of Allah which is based on common practice" — that is, an argument any person can follow from ordinary experience of how authority works — and adds that it is also a logical proof of the oneness of Allah, one that a great deal of literature explains in the books of theology (ʿilm al-kalām, the discipline of reasoned creedal argument). The reasoning runs:

- If there were two gods, each independent and sovereign, then the commands of both would have to prevail in the heavens and the earth.
- That is not possible, because it is inconceivable that two independent wills would hold common views on every matter.
- Differences of opinion are inevitable where power is shared; differences bring conflict, and conflict "would always lead to chaos and confusion."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then closes the obvious escape route. Could the two gods simply consult each other before issuing any command? That suggestion, it notes, has been adequately discussed and rejected in the books of theology, and the reason is beautifully simple: **if two gods had to take decisions jointly, then neither of them would have been sovereign — and a god with divided sovereignty is not a true deity.** A deity who must check with someone else has already ceased to be a deity. The very act of coordination is an admission of limitation.

The ayah does not end in argument but in praise: *"Glorified be Allah, the Lord of the Throne, above all that they associate with Him."* Ibn Kathir explains: "glorified be He above what they say about Him having offspring or partners; glorified and exalted and sanctified be He far above all the lies that they fabricate." That is what *tasbīḥ* — declaring Allah far above every falsehood spoken of Him — actually does here. It is not decoration at the end of a proof. It is what belongs in the mouth of a believer once falsehood about Allah has been named for what it is: not smugness at having won a debate, but reverence — *subḥān Allāh*, far above that. And notice the title Allah gives Himself at exactly this point in the argument about ultimate authority: **Lord of the Throne.**

The next ayah presses the same point from the side of accountability: *"He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will all be questioned."*

Ibn Kathir: "He is the Ruler Whose rule cannot be overturned and none can object to it, because of His might, majesty, pride, knowledge, wisdom, justice and subtlety." Read that whole list carefully, because it prevents a misunderstanding. Allah is not beyond objection merely because He is stronger than any objector. Might, majesty, knowledge, wisdom, justice and fine-grained care are all named together — there is no gap in such a decree through which a valid objection could enter.

The second half of the ayah reverses the direction completely: **"while they will be questioned."** Ibn Kathir: "He is the One Who will ask His creation about what they did," as in *"So, by your Lord, We shall certainly call all of them to account. For all that they used to do"* (15:92–93). He brings alongside it *"And He protects all, while against Whom there is no protector"* (23:88). Everything runs one way: shelter comes from Him, and nothing shelters from Him; accountability rises to Him, and none rises above Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows how this serves the passage's larger case — the ayah probably reinforces the argument that anyone who is answerable for his actions to someone else cannot be a true deity. Every proposed rival stands somewhere in the line of the questioned. Only One stands outside it.

There is a quiet mercy in this for anyone wrestling with a decree they do not understand. Ibn Kathir's list is the answer: what looks arbitrary from inside a life is issued from perfect knowledge, wisdom and justice. And our own station is the second half of the ayah — we will be asked. Better to spend our energy preparing an answer than demanding one.

## "Bring your proof"

Now the challenge becomes direct: *"Or have they taken other gods besides Him? Say: Bring your proof."*

Ibn Kathir glosses the demand simply — "your evidence for what you are saying." Note who is being asked. The burden falls on the one asserting a second god. And by the end of this passage Ibn Kathir states the outcome plainly: "the idolators have no proof and their dispute is of no use before their Lord; on them is wrath, and for them will be a severe torment."

Then Allah names the evidence on His own side: *"This is the Reminder (dhikr) for those with me and the Reminder for those before me."* Ibn Kathir reads "the Reminder for those with me" as **the Qur'an**, and "the Reminder for those before me" as **the previous Books** — "unlike what you claim. Each Book was revealed to each Prophet who was sent with the message that there is no god except Allah, but you idolators do not recognize the truth, so you turn away from it."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two readings of the phrase.** On the first, *dhikr* means "Message": the Message with the Prophet ﷺ is the Qur'an, and the Message of those before is the Torah, the Injīl (Evangel) and the Zabūr (Psalms). The conclusion is striking — neither the Qur'an nor the older books contain anything to suggest the worship of anyone but Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail worth pausing on: despite the fact that the texts of the Torah and Injīl have been altered, it is not suggested in either of them that Allah has partners with whom He shares His authority. On the second reading, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes to *Al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ*, *dhikr* here means "description": the Qur'an is a description for the people of the Prophet's ﷺ own day, setting out for them the rules of the Sharīʿah and inviting them to the correct way of life, and at the same time a description of those who came before, because it keeps alive the stories and traditions of peoples long gone.

The final ayah widens the evidence to its fullest reach: *"We never sent a messenger before you without revealing to him: There is no god but I, so worship Me."* Ibn Kathir places two parallels beside it — *"And ask those of Our Messengers whom We sent before you: Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious?"* (43:45), and *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger, proclaiming: Worship Allah, and avoid Ṭāghūt"* — all false deities — (16:36). His summary is exactly the passage's verdict: "Every Prophet who was sent by Allah called people to worship Allah Alone, with no partner or associate."

And then one witness more: **"The natural inclination of man (Al-Fiṭrah) also bears witness to that."** So the case closes with revelation and human nature testifying to the same thing. Idolatry is not merely unproven from outside; it is contradicted by something the worshipper already carries within.

## Living it

**Audit what you lean on.** The first ayah asks one blunt question of every rival: can it give life and raise the dead? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's conclusion is the standard to apply — only a Being with these powers is worthy of being worshipped.

**Let order be a reminder.** The argument of 21:22 is one anyone can follow from ordinary experience: divided sovereignty would mean disagreement, and disagreement chaos. That the heavens and the earth have not fallen into disorder is itself testimony to a single, unopposed rule.

**Take your place among the questioned.** Ayah 23 fixes the relationship: Allah asks; creation answers. Meet His decree trusting the perfection Ibn Kathir lists — knowledge, wisdom, justice, subtlety — and prepare your reply rather than your objection.

**Notice where the burden of proof lies.** "Bring your proof" is addressed to the one claiming a second god, and Ibn Kathir records the result: they have none.

**Stand in a very long line.** When you say *lā ilāha illā Allāh*, you are saying what every messenger before was sent to say — and, as Ibn Kathir notes, what the fiṭrah within you already bears witness to.

passages.title: Angels are servants, not divine offspring
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath:** these four ayat answer a single false claim — that the angels are Allah's children — not by argument alone, but by showing us the angels as they actually are: honoured servants who do not speak before their Master speaks, who move only at His command, who live in awe of Him, and who could never be mistaken for His offspring by anyone who truly saw them.

What holds ayat 26–29 together is that they are one continuous portrait. Ayah 26 states the claim and rejects it; ayat 27 and 28 describe the angels' conduct so that the rejection becomes self-evident; ayah 29 closes the door with a supposition that need never occur at all. The argument does not shout. It simply describes.

## The claim being answered

Ibn Kathir gives this passage the heading: the refutation of those who claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah, and a description of their deeds and status. Here, he explains, Allah refutes those who claimed He has offspring among the angels — exalted and sanctified be He. Some of the Arabs, he says, believed that the angels were the daughters of Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names them the same way: this was the claim of the pagans of Makkah.

That is the specific belief in view. It was not an abstract philosophical error; it was a live doctrine among the very people the Prophet ﷺ was addressing.

## "Glory to Him"

In ayah 26 the claim is quoted and immediately met with **سُبْحَانَهُ** — *subḥānahu*, "Glory to Him."

This is worth sitting with. Ibn Kathir's own aside as he introduces the refutation — "exalted and sanctified be He" — is the same instinct in miniature. The claim that Allah has a child is not treated as merely a factual slip to be corrected; it is met first with a declaration that Allah is far above it. The believer who hears something unworthy said of Allah may well feel that recoil before he feels the urge to debate.

## "Rather — honoured servants" (ayah 26)

Then comes the correction: **بَلۡ عِبَادٞ مُّكۡرَمُونَ**, *bal ʿibādun mukramūn* — "They are but honoured servants."

The little word *bal* ("rather", "on the contrary") does the work of a hinge. It does not merely deny; it replaces. You said *children* — no: **servants**.

But servanthood here is not humiliation. Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that the angels are servants of Allah who are honoured by Him and who hold high positions of noble status, and who obey Him to the utmost in all their words and deeds.

Read that carefully, because it reframes everything. Their honour is something Allah confers on them — they are *honoured by Him* — and it sits alongside obedience "to the utmost in all their words and deeds." The angels are creatures of noble status and the most thoroughly obedient, and in Ibn Kathir's description those two facts arrive together in a single sentence, not in tension.

## Two directions of obedience (ayah 27)

Ayah 27 then breaks that obedience into its two halves — speech and action:

**لَا يَسۡبِقُونَهُۥ بِٱلۡقَوۡلِ** — rendered by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "They do not precede Him in speech", and by Ibn Kathir as "They speak not until He has spoken." Either way the picture is the same: the angels never get ahead of Allah with a word.

**وَهُم بِأَمۡرِهِۦ يَعۡمَلُونَ** — "and they act on His command."

Ibn Kathir's gloss on the pair is exact: it means they do not initiate any matter before Him or go against His commands; on the contrary, they hasten to do as He commands. So it is not passivity. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same thing as waiting: they simply await His words and act accordingly.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the refutation explicit, turning it into a question: how can the angels be Allah's children when they stand in such awe in His presence that they neither initiate any talk nor act against His commands? This is the conduct of servants, and it is visible for anyone honest enough to look.

## He encompasses them (ayah 28)

Ibn Kathir joins the end of ayah 27 to what follows: He encompasses them with His knowledge, so that nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him. Ayah 28 states it: **يَعۡلَمُ مَا بَيۡنَ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ وَمَا خَلۡفَهُمۡ** — "He knows what is before them, and what is behind them."

The image is spatial and total: whatever lies ahead of the angels and whatever lies behind them is inside His knowledge. Nothing of them is hidden from Him.

## Intercession is permission, not leverage

Then: **وَلَا يَشۡفَعُونَ إِلَّا لِمَنِ ٱرۡتَضَىٰ** — "and they cannot intercede except for him with whom He is pleased."

Ibn Kathir places this alongside two other ayat that say the same thing: *"Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?"* (2:255), and *"Intercession with Him profits not except for him whom He permits"* (34:23) — and he notes that there are many ayat which say similar things.

Intercession, then, is real — but as these ayat state it, it runs on Allah's permission and reaches the one with whom He is pleased. Which means the way to be interceded for is to be someone with whom Allah is pleased.

## Awe as their permanent state

**وَهُم مِّنۡ خَشۡيَتِهِۦ مُشۡفِقُونَ** — Ibn Kathir explains "and they for fear of Him" as meaning *because they fear Him*, and *mushfiqūn* as their standing in awe. So their trembling is not vague dread; it is caused by Him.

Hold this next to *mukramūn* from ayah 26. The same beings Ibn Kathir describes as honoured by Allah and holding high positions of noble status are described here as standing in awe of Him. Height of station and depth of awe belong to the same creatures.

## The impossible supposition (ayah 29)

Ayah 29 closes the argument at its furthest edge: **وَمَن يَقُلۡ مِنۡهُمۡ إِنِّيٓ إِلَٰهٞ مِّن دُونِهِۦ فَذَٰلِكَ نَجۡزِيهِ جَهَنَّمَ** — "And if any of them should say: 'Verily, I am a god besides Him,' such We should recompense with Hell. Thus We recompense the wrongdoers."

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning whoever claims to be a god instead of Allah, that is, alongside Allah; and "thus We recompense the wrongdoers" means everyone who says this.

Then comes the point that saves the ayah from being misread. Ibn Kathir notes: **this is a conditional sentence, and the condition stated does not necessarily have to take place.** The ayah is not reporting that some angel might rebel. It is stating what such a claim would earn.

Ibn Kathir supports this with two parallels of the same kind: *"Say: 'If the Most Gracious had a son, then I am the first of worshippers'"* (43:81), and *"If you join others in worship with Allah, then surely all your deeds will be in vain, and you will certainly be among the losers"* (39:65).

There is also something quiet in how ayah 29 ends. It does not say "thus We recompense the angels who claim this"; it says **thus We recompense the wrongdoers** — and Ibn Kathir reads that as: everyone who says this. The judgement is stated as a rule, without exception. No status, however exalted, buys an exemption.

## Living it

**Correct speech about Allah is an act of worship.** The passage begins with a false sentence about Allah and answers it with *subḥānahu*. When we hear Allah spoken of in a way that lowers Him, the first response is to declare Him far above it.

**Honour and service belong together.** Ibn Kathir describes the angels in one breath as honoured by Allah, holding high positions of noble status, and obeying Him to the utmost in all their words and deeds. Whoever wants rank with Allah should look for it where the angels' description places it.

**Do not run ahead.** Ayah 27's picture — servants who do not initiate any matter before Him, who await His words, and who then hasten to do as He commands — is a whole discipline of the heart: not putting our preferences ahead of His command, and once the command is clear, moving quickly.

**An etiquette drawn from ayah 27.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a point of manners from this same ayah: it points to an important etiquette of behaving in the company of elders — when a matter is brought before a group, people should wait until the elder among them has spoken before speaking themselves, since speaking before the elder is contrary to the manners governing respect of elders. It is a small, concrete thing, and it is striking where it comes from: the way the angels behave before Allah casts a shadow all the way down into how we behave in a room.

**Seek to be someone Allah is pleased with.** Since intercession reaches only "him with whom He is pleased", and only by Allah's permission, the surer path is becoming the kind of person for whom it would be permitted.

**Let knowledge of Him produce awe.** He knows what is before the angels and what is behind them, and they, for fear of Him, stand in awe. That awe is the response of creatures who know Him best.

passages.title: Cosmic signs for those who see
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are a single sustained argument. Allah turns the disbelievers' attention to the sky over their heads and the ground under their feet, and puts one question to them: how can you look at all of this and still worship anything besides the One who made it? Ibn Kathir opens his comment on the whole passage by saying that here Allah tells of His perfect might and power in His creation and subjugation of all things. Ayah 30 gives the origin of the world and of life; ayah 31 the earth made liveable; ayah 32 the sky raised and guarded; ayah 33 the great clock of night, day, sun and moon. Four exhibits, one verdict — and the sting in the middle of it is ayah 32: **they walk under all of it and turn away.**

## "Have they not seen?"

The passage opens with أَوَلَمْ يَرَ — *a-wa-lam yara*, "have they not seen." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *ruʼyat* (seeing) is used here in its general sense — knowledge, whether it is acquired by visual observation or arrived at by logical conclusion. And it adds that the discussion which follows refers partly to actual observation and partly to logical inference. So Allah is not asking only for eyesight. He is asking for the kind of seeing that draws a conclusion.

Ibn Kathir explains who is being addressed: *those who disbelieve* means those who deny His divine nature and worship others instead of Him. And he puts the argument in the form of a question — do they not realise that Allah is the One who is independent in His powers of creation, and who runs the affairs of all things with absolute power? So how can it be appropriate to worship anything beside Him, or to associate others with Him in worship? The cosmos is not being described here as a wonder for its own sake. It is being submitted as evidence for *tawḥīd* — that Allah alone deserves worship, because Allah alone created and sustains.

## Ratq and fatq: closed, then opened

Everything in ayah 30 turns on two Arabic words. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives them plainly: **رَتْق (ratq) means to close, and فَتْق (fatq) means to open.** Used in combination, it says, the two words together convey *full control* in the management and execution of a task — the one who closes a thing and then opens it is the one who has it entirely in his hand.

Commentators explained the closing and the opening in more than one way. The meaning adopted by the Companions of the Holy Prophet ﷺ and by the majority of the exegetes, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is this: **the sky was "closed" in the sense that it shut off rainfall, and the earth was "closed" in the sense that nothing grew from it; the "opening" was the opening of these two — the rainfall and the vegetation.** On this reading the ayah is describing something you can still watch happening every spring.

The source for that reading is one of the most beautiful exchanges in the tafsir tradition, recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim and related in both our sources. A man came to Ibn ʿUmar and asked him about this ayah — about the heavens and earth being joined and then parted. Ibn ʿUmar did not answer. He said: go to that old man (that *Shaykh*) and ask him, then come back and tell me what he says to you. So the man went to Ibn ʿAbbas, who told him: "Yes, the heavens were joined together and it did not rain, and the earth was joined together and nothing grew. When living beings were created to populate the earth, rain came forth from the heavens and vegetation came forth from the earth." The man returned and repeated it. Ibn ʿUmar said: "Now I know that Ibn ʿAbbas has been given knowledge of the Qurʼan. He has spoken the truth, and this is how it was." And then he added the line that makes the story unforgettable — "I did not like the daring attitude of Ibn ʿAbbas in his tafsir of the Qurʼan, but now I know that he has been given knowledge of the Qurʼan."

Notice the shape of the story: Ibn ʿUmar sent the questioner to hear the interpretation, weighed it when it came back to him, and then named the reservation he had held and withdrew it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this report of Ibn ʿAbbas is also carried in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī through Ibn Mundhir and Abū Nuʿaim, and that a group of the scholars of hadith including Ḥākim, the writer of the *Mustadrak*, accepted the narration as correct. Ibn ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAufī judged this interpretation *ḥasan* — good — and comprehensive, and compatible with the text of the Qurʼan: it contains a lesson and an argument against the disbelievers, and it mentions the Omnipotence and the special bounties of Allah, which are the basis of His Oneness and of the recognition of His attributes. The sentence that follows in the same ayah — "and We created from water every living thing" — also corroborates this interpretation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that al-Baḥr ul-Muḥīṭ adopted the same interpretation, that Qurṭubī declared this explanation to be that of ʿIkrimah as well and said another ayah endorses the meaning, and that Ṭabarī adopted this very interpretation too.

**A second reading.** Ibn Kathir takes the words to the beginning of things: the heavens and the earth were joined together, in the beginning all one piece, attached to one another and piled up on top of one another, and then He separated them — making the heavens seven and the earth seven, and placing the air between the earth and the lowest heaven. Then He caused rain to fall from the sky and vegetation to grow from the earth. He cites the early authorities on this: Saʿīd bin Jubayr said, "The heavens and the earth were attached to one another, then when the heavens were raised up, the earth became separate from them, and this is their parting which was mentioned by Allah in His Book." Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said, "They were joined together, then they were separated by this air."

Ibn Kathir also preserves a striking piece of reasoning from Ibn ʿAbbas, narrated by Sufyān ath-Thawrī from his father from ʿIkrimah. Ibn ʿAbbas was asked which came first, the night or the day. He answered with a question: do you think that when the heavens and the earth were joined together, there was anything between them except darkness? Thus you may know that the night came before the day.

**And a caution.** Muhammad Taqi Usmani notes in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān that this is part of the miraculous style of the Qurʼan — the words it uses may carry more than one possibility of interpretation. *Ratq* and *fatq* also mean "being compact" and "being separated," in which case the ayah may be translated, "The heavens and the earth were compact, then We separated them," referring to an event of the early creation in which the heavens and the earth were originally a single body, after which Allah separated the earth from the heavens. He observes that contemporary research about the Big Bang is close to this description — and then immediately adds the guardrail every reader should memorise: **the Qurʼanic descriptions are independent of any scientific theory, and the Qurʼan should not be made subject to ever-changing theories.** Take the confirmation gratefully; do not stake the Book on a model that may be revised next decade.

## "And We made from water every living thing"

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and total: **the origin of every living thing is in water.** And he reads the closing question of ayah 30 — *afalā yuʼminūn*, "will they not then believe?" — as pressing on something people see with their own eyes: they see how creation develops step by step, and all of that is proof of the existence of the Creator who is in control of all things and able to do whatever He wills. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that water is an essential element in the creation of all living things, playing a very important role in the creation, growth and evolution of everything alive.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records here a narration from Imam Ahmad, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "O Messenger of Allah, when I see you I feel happy and content — tell me about everything." The Prophet ﷺ said, **"Everything was created from water."** Abu Hurayrah then asked him about something which, if he did it, would take him into Paradise. The Prophet ﷺ said: **"Spread the greeting of Salām, feed others, uphold the ties of kinship, and stand in prayer at night when people are sleeping. Then you will enter Paradise in peace."**

Ibn Kathir comments on the chain: it fulfils the conditions of the Two Ṣaḥīḥs apart from Abu Maymūnah — whose first name was Sālim, and who is one of the men of the *Sunans* — and At-Tirmidhī classed him as *ṣaḥīḥ*.

Sit with the shape of that exchange. A man asks about how everything was made and is told, in a few words, where everything comes from. Then he asks the question that actually matters for him — what gets me to Paradise? — and is given four ordinary, repeatable deeds: greet people, feed people, keep family ties, pray at night. The cosmology and the practice belong to one conversation.

## The earth made liveable (ayah 31)

**رَوَاسِيَ (rawāsī)** — firmly anchored mountains. Ibn Kathir explains that these are mountains which stabilise the earth, keep it steady and lend it weight, lest it should shake with the people — that is, move and tremble so that they would not be able to stand firm on it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the verb: **مَيْد (mayd) in Arabic means to be convulsed**, so the meaning of the ayah is that Allah has planted mountains on the earth to hold it in place, because any violent movement of the earth would be catastrophic to those who live on it.

Ibn Kathir also draws attention to a detail easily skipped: the earth is covered with water apart from one-quarter of its surface, so the land is exposed to the air and the sun — so that its people may see the sky with its dazzling signs and evidence.

Then the second half of the ayah: **فِجَاجًا سُبُلًا** — broad ways to travel through.
