Then, immediately: **ثُمَّ نُكِسُوا۟ عَلَىٰ رُءُوسِهِمْ** — and Ibn Kathir gives the phrase a very human sense: it means "they looked at the ground." The flash of clarity in the previous ayah does not survive; the eyes go down. Anyone who has watched a person lose an argument they cannot afford to lose knows this posture exactly.

And from that lowered posture they say: **"Indeed you know well that these speak not!"** Qatadah's comment, quoted by Ibn Kathir, catches the tone: "The people admitted their guilt and confusion," and their words mean — *so how can you tell us to ask them, if they cannot speak and you know that they cannot speak?* It is meant as a rebuke to Ibrahim. It is in fact a confession. Under pressure they have said out loud, in public, before their whole assembly, the one fact about their gods that ruins everything: these things cannot talk.

That is why Ibrahim's earlier words were so devastating. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains — following al-Bahr ul-Muhit, Qurtubi and Ruh ul-Maʿani — that when Ibrahim said "rather, this is done by this chief of theirs," it was *isnād majāzī*, a metaphoric attribution: the deed was ascribed to the big idol because it was the reverence that this idol commanded in the whole community which drove Ibrahim to do what he did to the smaller ones. The commentary compares it to the Arabic saying "the spring rains have raised the crops" — in actual fact it is Allah who produces and nourishes the crops, yet the deed is ascribed to a visible cause, and no one calls that a lie. Ibrahim had also placed an axe on the big idol's shoulder or in its hands, pointing an accusing finger. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists what this served: it invited them to wonder whether the big idol was infuriated with the smaller ones because they were worshipped with the same reverence as itself — and if even that idol would not accept partners in worship, how could Allah, the Creator of all living things, agree to share His authority with anyone? It invited them to wonder how idols as powerful as they imagined could be broken with impunity. And if the charge could be laid against the chief, then he ought to have the power of speech to answer it.

**A word on the famous hadith.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses the report — which it cites as being in Bukhari and Muslim — that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) never spoke an untruth except on three occasions: his words about the chief idol here, "I am sick" (37:89), and calling Sayyidah Sarah his sister before a cruel and depraved ruler. The commentary's answer is that the hadith refutes the charge from within itself: none of the three episodes reveals that a deliberate lie was told. Each was *tauriyah* — dissembling, where the words used may be interpreted differently, so that the listener understands them one way while the speaker means something else. Sarah truly was his sister in the wider sense of Muslim brotherhood, the two of them being the only Muslims in that land; *saqīm* in common parlance means "sick" but also means depressed, dejected, despondent and weak, which was absolutely true of his feelings among the unbelievers; and the deed truly did belong to the chief idol by metaphoric attribution. Tauriyah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is permissible by the consensus of the jurists when used to save oneself from injustice — and is totally different from the Shiite doctrine of *taqiyyah*, in which one not only speaks a lie but acts on it.

Why, then, does the hadith call them lies at all? Because the slightest slip of those who are close to Allah is taken seriously. In the famous and well-known hadith of *shafāʿah* — the great intercession — every prophet will excuse himself on the Day of Resurrection by recounting one or more of his slips, and Ibrahim will excuse himself by quoting these utterances, which, though tauriyah and therefore not lies in actual fact, were nonetheless below the dignity of a prophet. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the boundary clearly: apart from quoting the Qur'an or this hadith, no one is permitted to say that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) told a lie. It also warns against the opposite error — rejecting a report whose narrators are reliable because we imagine it clashes with the Qur'an. The principle that a report conflicting with the Qur'an is to be rejected is itself valid and accepted by the whole Ummah; the point is that the scholars spent their entire lives researching each and every hadith, and none of what they accepted as authentic conflicts with the Qur'an. And there is a further, quieter observation the commentary reproduces from Qurtubi, from Qazi Abu Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabi: of the three, the two spoken for Allah's sake are described as such, but the third — protecting his wife — is not, because there was in it an element of personal interest as well. For men like us the act would have counted as done for Allah; but in prophets, the smallest degree of personal motive was weighed against the perfection of their devotion.

With the confession on the record, Ibrahim strikes: **"Do you then worship besides Allah, things that can neither profit you nor harm you?"** Ibn Kathir puts the logic plainly: if they cannot speak, and can neither benefit you nor harm you, then why do you worship them instead of Allah? Benefit and harm are the whole reason anyone worships anything. Strip those away and worship has no object left.

Then: **أُفٍّ لَّكُمْ وَلِمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ** — "Fie upon you, and upon that which you worship besides Allah!" Notice that his revulsion falls on two things at once — the idols, and the choice the people made. This is not contempt for their persons but horror at what they have done to themselves, which is why it ends in a question rather than a curse: **أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ** — "Have you then no sense?" Ibn Kathir paraphrases: do you not realize the extent of the misguidance and extreme disbelief which you are following, which no one could accept but one who is an ignorant and evil wrongdoer? And he closes the movement with a verdict: "He defeated them in argument and left them with no way out," citing Allah's own word on the episode — *"And that was Our proof which We gave Ibrahim against his people"* (6:83). The victory in this scene belongs to a proof that Allah gave.

## The fire (68–69)

Ibn Kathir marks the transition exactly: "When their arguments were refuted and their incapability became clear, when truth was made manifest and falsehood was defeated, they resorted to using their power and strength." **"Burn him and help your gods, if you will be doing."** The slogan is telling — the gods who could not guard themselves now need their worshippers to defend *them*.

What follows is a portrait of a whole society mobilised for one execution. "So they gathered together a huge amount of wood," Ibn Kathir says. As-Suddi reports that a woman who fell ill would vow that if she recovered she would bring wood to burn Ibrahim — piety itself repurposed as fuel. They made a hole in the ground and set it aflame, and it burned with huge sparks and immense flames; there had never been a fire like it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates the historical account of the scale: the entire population of the city spent a full month collecting firewood, and once it was lit they fanned it for seven days until the flames rose high into the sky. And then the absurdity at the heart of it — the fire burned with such intensity that no one dared approach it. As-Suddi reports that they put Ibrahim into a catapult, at the suggestion of a nomadic Kurdish man from Persia; Shuʿayb al-Jabaʾi names him Hayzan and says Allah caused the earth to swallow him up, and he will remain sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection. In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account it was Shaytan who supplied the idea of the catapult.

**Sufficient for me is Allah.** As they prepared to throw Allah's Friend (*khalīl*) into that sea of fire, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that all the angels and all the creatures of the earth and sky cried out in unison at what lay in store for him, and Allah permitted them all to come to his aid. When the angels asked whether he needed their help, he replied that Allah was enough to help him and that He was watching over him. When Jibra'il al-Ameen (peace be upon him) asked whether he could render him any help, he answered, "Of course I need help, but from Allah, not from you."

And as they threw him he said: **"Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best disposer of affairs."** Ibn Kathir notes this in Shuʿayb al-Jabaʾi's report, and adds that it is similar to what Al-Bukhari recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas — that Ibrahim said these words when he was thrown into the fire, and that Muhammad ﷺ said them too, when it was said to the believers: *"Verily, the people have gathered against you, therefore, fear them. But it increased them in faith, and they said: حَسْبُنَا ٱللَّهُ وَنِعْمَ ٱلْوَكِيلُ — 'Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs'"* (3:173). The same sentence, in the mouth of the *khalīl* of Allah and in the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers with him. The sources do not leave that as a coincidence for you to notice — it is the point.

**قُلْنَا يَا نَارُ كُونِي بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا عَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ** — "We said: 'O fire! Be you cool and safety for Ibrahim!'"

No rescue party arrives. Allah addresses the fire directly, and the fire obeys. Saʿid bin Jubayr reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said: when Ibrahim was thrown into the fire, the angel in charge of rain said, "When will I be commanded to send rain?" — but the command of Allah was more swift. And in the same report: "there was no fire left on earth that was not extinguished."

**Why "and safety" had to be said.** This is the detail at which both commentaries stop. Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-ʿAliyah said: were it not for the fact that Allah said *wa salāman*, "and safety," Ibrahim would have been harmed by its coldness. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — had the word *bard* ("cool") not been followed by the word *salām* ("safe"), the fire would have cooled like ice and would have caused him harm. Allah's mercy is exact: He does not merely reverse the danger, He measures the reversal so that the cure does not become a second affliction.

**How did it happen?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports two views: that the fire ceased to be fire and changed into a pleasant breeze, or — the explanation it considers more plausible — that the fire remained fire and went on burning the things around him but did not touch his body, so much so that it even burnt down the rope that bound him. Either way, it adds, citing Mazhari, that according to some historical accounts he remained in the fire seven days, and used to recall that those seven days were the most comfortable time of his entire life.

**A note for the sceptic.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers those who do not believe in miracles, and the answer is worth following. The philosophical assumption that attributes attached to a thing are inseparable from it is itself fallacious; nothing in this world is essential to or inseparable from something else. Allah gave fire the attribute of burning and water the attribute of cooling, but these attributes are customary and habitual, not rationally necessary — no philosopher has been able to advance a convincing argument that they are. Being merely habitual, they can be changed whenever Allah so wills: fire can act as a coolant and water as a burning agent, and this cannot be held rationally impossible. This is what happens when Allah reveals His miracles in support of the missions of His prophets. As evidence that the pairing can run the other way too, the commentary cites what the Qur'an says of the people of Nuh (peace be upon him): *"they were drowned, and admitted into a Fire"* (71:25).

**Qatadah's observation** adds a small, strange, moving detail: on that day there was no creature that did not try to extinguish the fire for Ibrahim, except for the gecko. Az-Zuhri said that the Prophet ﷺ commanded that it should be killed, and called it a harmful vermin.

## The verdict (70)

**وَأَرَادُوا۟ بِهِۦ كَيْدًا فَجَعَلْنَٰهُمُ ٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ** — "And they wanted to harm him, but We made them the worst losers."

Ibn Kathir's comment is compact: they were defeated and humiliated, because they wanted to plot against the Prophet of Allah, but Allah planned against them and saved him from the fire, and thus they were defeated. Against a man they had already lost to in open argument they resorted to a plot; and against Allah, a plot is the least useful thing a person can own.

Weigh what they spent. A month of gathering wood. Seven days of fanning. The vows of the sick. A whole city's labour, and a fire the like of which had never been seen — and at the end of it Ibrahim comes out with the rope burned off him and his Lord vindicated in front of everyone, while they are left as **ٱلْأَخْسَرِينَ**, "the worst losers." The word is a superlative, and it is deliberate: it is not merely that their scheme failed, but that no one lost more by scheming than they did.

## Living it

- **Notice the half-confession.** They did admit a wrong — the wrong of poor security. It is easy to concede the small fault that shields us from admitting the large one. When conscience stirs, let the thought finish.
- **Argument first, and argument honestly.** Ibrahim did not begin with force; he brought his people to say the truth out loud themselves. Ibn Kathir's summary is the model — he defeated them in argument and left them with no way out — and even that, Allah calls *Our* proof which *We* gave him (6:83). Clarity is a gift, not a talent.
- **Learn the sentence he said as they threw him in.** "Sufficient for me is Allah, and He is the best disposer of affairs." It was enough for Ibrahim in the catapult and enough for the believers when the people had gathered against them (3:173). It is made for the moment when the help you can see has run out.
- **Ask Allah first, not the means.** Offered aid by the angels and by Jibra'il himself, Ibrahim's answer was that his need was real but his asking went to Allah alone. He was not refusing help; he was refusing to let any helper take Allah's place.
- **Trust the "and safety."** Allah's rescue is measured to the exact degree. Had "cool" come without "safe," the cold itself would have harmed him. When Allah lifts a hardship, He does not hand you its opposite to suffer instead.

passages.title: Deliverance of Abraham, Lot and Noah
passages.tafsir:
This passage is about rescue. Three prophets — Ibrahim, Lut and Nuh — are each lifted out of a hostile people, and in every case the deliverance is followed by a gift: a blessed land, children and grandchildren, wisdom and knowledge, entry into Allah's mercy, victory over the deniers.

**What holds these ayat together.** One verb runs through the whole unit like a thread. In ayah 71, of Ibrahim, *wa najjaynāhu* — "and We delivered him"; in ayah 74, of Lut, *wa najjaynāhu* again; in ayah 76, of Nuh, *fa najjaynāhu*. The same root, the same divine actor, three different eras. The passage is not three separate stories placed side by side; it is one statement made three times: **when a servant of Allah is cornered, Allah is the one who gets him out.**

And notice the shape of the sentences. *We delivered, We bestowed, We made, We revealed, We admitted, We answered, We helped, We drowned.* In every clause the prophets are on the receiving end. Allah is the one acting.

## First: taken out — and then taken somewhere

Ibn Kathir explains ayah 71 by telling us what came just before it: Allah saved Ibrahim from the fire lit by his people, and then brought him out from among them altogether, migrating to the land of ash-Shām, to the sacred regions thereof.

So deliverance came in two stages. First he was saved from the burning. Then Allah moved him. Being rescued was not the end of it; Ibrahim was not returned to the life he had been living. He was taken somewhere better.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the geography: Ibrahim and Lut were delivered from ʿIrāq, the land where Namrūd ruled, and sent to the peaceful land of Syria — and that word "peaceful" is doing real work after everything Ibrahim had just endured.

**"The land We had blessed for all the worlds."** Why *lil-ʿālamīn* — for all the worlds, not just for Ibrahim, not just for its own people? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that Allah's bounties were in abundance there, not only for the locals but for the people of the world, and that this land holds two kinds of blessing:

- **Inward blessing** — many prophets were born in that land. That is a bounty belonging to humanity as a whole, not to a region.
- **Outward blessing** — a moderate climate, natural beauty, greenery, springs and streams all around, sustaining a large variety of vegetation, fruits and flowers.

Hold the two halves together and the phrase opens up. A land is genuinely blessed when it feeds bodies *and* produces guidance. The Qur'an does not treat the streams and the prophets as belonging to two different categories of gift; both are named as blessing.

The same two-stage pattern governs the other two rescues. Lut is saved *from* the town (ayah 74) and then *"admitted into Our mercy"* (ayah 75). Nuh is saved *from* the great distress (ayah 76) and then *"helped against the people"* (ayah 77). The passage never stops at the escape. Every deliverance in it opens onto something given.

## The gift that went beyond the asking

Ibrahim had been brought out from among his own people and away from his homeland. Ayah 72 is Allah giving him a family: *"And We bestowed upon him Isḥāq, and Yaʿqūb as nāfilah."*

**What does *nāfilah* mean here?** The commentators give two complementary readings, and Ibn Kathir preserves both:

- **ʿAṭāʼ and Mujāhid** said *nāfilatan* means "as a gift" — freely given.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and al-Ḥakam ibn ʿUyaynah** said it means "the gift of a son who has a son" — that is, Yaʿqūb was the son of Isḥāq, so what Ibrahim received was not merely a child but a line. Ibn Kathir supports this by pointing to Allah's words elsewhere: *"But We gave her glad tidings of Isḥāq, and after Isḥāq, of Yaʿqūb"* (11:71).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the linguistic root of it: Allah gave him the son Isḥāq in answer to his supplication, and in addition a grandson, Yaʿqūb, as a gift — which is why the word used is *nāfilah*, which originally means **"extra."**

And here is where the ayah becomes moving. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam pointed out that Ibrahim had asked for **one**: *"My Lord! Grant me from the righteous"* (37:100). Allah gave him Isḥāq — that was the answer to the duʿāʼ — **and then gave him Yaʿqūb in addition.** The grandson was not in the request. He was the *extra*.

That is the shape of divine generosity this passage wants you to see: the prayer is answered, and then something is added that you never thought to ask for.

**"Each one We made righteous."** Ibn Kathir explains this simply: both of them were good and righteous people. The gift was not only that sons were born, but that they turned out well — which is itself something only Allah gives. And note that *ṣāliḥīn*, "the righteous," is the exact word used again of Lut three ayat later (*"truly, he was of the righteous"*). The passage keeps returning to that one quality as the thing that matters about a person.

## What Allah made of the ones He delivered

The rescued are not simply left in safety. Ayah 73 describes what Allah made of this family, and it repays reading phrase by phrase, as Ibn Kathir reads it:

**"And We made them leaders" (*aʼimmah*)** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, *examples to be followed*.

**"guiding by Our command"** — Ibn Kathir glosses this as *inviting to Him by His leave*. The guidance is not theirs to invent. They call, and the calling itself proceeds from Allah's command and permission.

**"and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of ṣalāh, and the giving of zakāh"** — Ibn Kathir makes a precise observation here: **the general is followed by the specific.** "The doing of good deeds" covers everything; then out of that vast field two things are singled out and named.

**"and of Us alone they were the worshippers"** — and Ibn Kathir's comment on this closing phrase is the sting in the whole ayah: **they did what they enjoined others to do.**

That is what the passage puts at the end of the list. Everything before this clause described what they told people to do. This clause says they were doing it themselves.

The same pattern of endowment appears again one ayah later, with Lut: *"And to Lut We gave wisdom and knowledge."* Ibn Kathir gives us the man first — **Lut ibn Hārān ibn Āzar** — who believed in Ibrahim and followed him and migrated with him, as Allah says: *"So Lut believed in him. He (Ibrahim) said: 'I will emigrate for the sake of my Lord'"* (29:26).

Remember that when you read ayah 71, where the two of them are delivered together. Lut's story begins as someone else's follower. He left with Ibrahim, and Allah then gave him something of his own: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah gave him wisdom and knowledge, sent revelation to him, made him a prophet, and appointed him to Sadūm (Sodom) and its vicinity. They rejected him and resisted him, and so Allah utterly destroyed them.

## The towns that were left behind

Each rescue has a shadow: the people who would not be rescued.

**"the town which practised *al-khabāʼith*."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up this word carefully. *Khabāʼith* is the **plural** of *khabīthah*, meaning wickedness; too many wicked things taken collectively are called *khabāʼith*. Two explanations are offered for why the plural is used here:

- Their most abominable practice — one which, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, **even the animals do not indulge in** — was sodomy. It is possible, as some commentators have explained, that because of the extreme wickedness of this practice it is referred to in the plural rather than the singular: one deed weighed as though it were many.
- The second explanation, cited from *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*, is that the people of Sodom also indulged in other bad habits — drinking, singing, shaving off the beard and growing the moustache, wearing silk clothes, stone-throwing, whistling and the like — so the plural covers the whole spread of their conduct.

Either way, the point of the plural is that this was not an individual falling into a sin. This was a *town* — a settled culture of wrongdoing, with rejection of the prophet built into it. The Qur'an's own verdict follows immediately: *"Verily, they were a people given to evil, and were rebellious."*

**What happened to it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Ibn ʿAbbās as cited by al-Qurṭubī, that the city was Sodom, and that there were seven other townships under it, all of which were thrown upside down by Jibrāʼīl (peace be upon him) — **except one, which was left intact for Lut and his followers.**

Sit with that exception. The destruction was total in its reach and yet exact in its aim. Allah did not save Lut *despite* the judgement; the judgement itself was shaped around him.

The verdict on Nuh's people at the end of the passage is worded almost identically — *"a people given to evil" (qawma sawʼ)* — the same description given to the people of Lut in ayah 74. Different era, different sin, the same sentence passed.

## The rescue that came before all of these

**"And Nuh, when he cried out earlier…"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word *min qablu*, "earlier": it means **before the time of Ibrahim and Lut**, whose account has just preceded in the previous verses. The passage is not moving forward in time here; it steps back behind everything you have just read to show that this pattern of deliverance is older still.

**The cry that is only hinted at.** Ayah 76 says merely that he "called". Both commentaries supply what he called with, from elsewhere in the Qur'an:

- *"I have been overcome, so help me!"* (54:10) — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes this came when his people would not listen to him at all.
- *"My Lord! Leave not any inhabitant of the disbelievers upon the earth! If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants, and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers"* (71:26–27).

Ibn Kathir introduces both of these as Nuh praying against his people for their disbelief in him — and the reason Nuh himself gives in the second is striking: not personal grievance, but what these people would do to *others* and to the generations they would produce.

**"and We saved him and his family."** Ibn Kathir is careful here: "his family" means **those who believed with him** — as Allah says elsewhere, *"…and your family — except him against whom the Word has already gone forth — and those who believe. And none believed with him except a few"* (11:40). In the reckoning of this rescue, the tie that counted was faith. One of his household, against whom the Word had already gone forth, was not among the saved.

**"from the great distress" (*al-karb al-ʿaẓīm*).** The sources give two readings:

- Ibn Kathir takes it as **difficulty, rejection and harm**, and then tells you what that meant in practice: Nuh remained among his people **a thousand years less fifty**, calling them to Allah, and no one believed in him except a few. His people were plotting against him and advising one another **century after century, generation after generation**, to oppose him. The "great distress" was not one dramatic night; it was 950 years of being disbelieved, with the hostility handed down from fathers to sons.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān allows that the "terrible agony" may refer either to the drowning of the deluge which annihilated the entire people, or to the torture which he and his followers suffered at the hands of those people.

**"And We helped him against the people."** Ibn Kathir reads *naṣarnāhu* as covering both halves at once: *We saved him and helped him against the people.* Rescue and victory in a single verb.

And then ayah 77 closes with the verdict: *"who denied Our signs. Verily, they were a people given to evil. So We drowned them all."* Ibn Kathir underlines the word *all*: Allah drowned them all, and not one of them was left on the face of the earth — **as their Prophet had prayed would happen to them.**

Set that against the nine and a half centuries. The duʿāʼ of a man nobody listened to, made after a lifetime of being denied, was answered so completely that the earth was cleared.

## Living it

Read as one unit, these seven ayat leave a believer with a handful of things to carry:

**Deliverance is Allah's act, not an accident.** In each of the three cases the escape is expressed as something Allah *did*, deliberately, to a named servant. Nothing here is left to circumstance.

**Being taken out is only half of it.** Ibrahim was taken out of the fire and into a blessed land. Lut was taken out of Sodom and into Allah's mercy. Nuh was taken out of the distress and given victory. The passage never stops at the escape.

**Ask, and expect the extra.** Ibrahim asked for a righteous son and received a righteous line. *Nāfilah* means what came beyond the asking.

**Practise what you call to.** Ayah 73 describes those Allah made leaders as examples to be followed, guiding by Allah's command, worshippers of Allah alone — because, as Ibn Kathir says, *they did what they enjoined others to do*.

**And when the response is nothing at all, keep calling.** Nuh gave 950 years to people who answered him with plotting, and then made a duʿāʼ that was answered without remainder. For anyone worn down by a call no one seems to be answering, the message of these ayat is that Allah has done this before, more than once, and He records the names of those He delivered.

passages.title: David and Solomon: judgment, armour, wind
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These five ayat present Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them) — father and son, both prophets, both rulers — through one courtroom scene and a list of extraordinary gifts.

**What holds them together.** Read the verbs. *We made Sulayman understand… to each We gave… We subjected… We taught him… We were guarding them.* Every capacity here is a grant, not an achievement. And the sequence is bracketed by two statements about Allah Himself: in ayah 78, "We were witness to their judgement," and in ayah 81, "And of everything We are the All-Knower." Two kings at the height of their powers, and the frame around them is Allah's knowledge.

## The case of the field (ayah 78)

**The word that sets the scene.** The ayah says the people's sheep *nafashat* in the field. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in Arabic *nafash* means an animal getting into a field **at night** and damaging it. Ibn Kathir gathers the early authorities: Ibn ʿAbbas said *nafash* means grazing; Shurayh, Az-Zuhri and Qatadah said it only happens at night — and Qatadah added that *al-haml* is grazing during the day.

**What was growing there.** The Qur'an says *al-harth*, the tilled crop. (Abu) Ishaq narrated from Murrah from Ibn Masʿud that it was grapes, the bunches dangling — Shurayh's view too.

## Two verdicts (ayat 78–79)

Ibn Jarir records from Ibn Masʿud — and Al-ʿAwfi the like from Ibn ʿAbbas — that Dawud ruled the owner of the grapes should keep the sheep. Sulayman said, "Not like this, O Prophet of Allah!" Dawud said, "How then?" Sulayman answered: give the grapes to the owner of the sheep to tend until they grow back as they were; give the sheep to the owner of the grapes to benefit from meanwhile; then each returns to its owner.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the detail Imam Baghawi reports on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and Zuhri. Two men came to Dawud: one owned a flock, the other a field of crops, and the second complained that the first's animals had got into his field at night and eaten the crop. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents it, the value of the flock was presumably equal to the value of the ruined crop, which makes Dawud's verdict straightforward jurisprudence: property destroyed is compensated at its price. The two men met Sulayman at the door on their way out; he told his father he would have judged differently, to the benefit of both: let the field's owner take the flock and live off its milk and wool, let the shepherd cultivate the field until it is restored to what it was, and then let each take back his own. Dawud approved it, called the men back, and announced the second judgement.

**Why the difference matters.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: Dawud's judgement was *not* in conflict with the sacred law. Sulayman's was inspired by Allah and was more appropriate because it benefited both parties without hurting either.

## "And We were witness to their judgement"

The scene ends with *wa kunna li-hukmihim shahidin*. Two prophets differ in open court, and Allah says He was present to it. Then ayah 79 gives the verdict on the verdicts: *fa-fahhamnaha Sulayman* — "We made Sulayman understand it" — immediately followed by *wa kullan atayna hukman wa ʿilman*, "and to each of them We gave wisdom and knowledge." Sulayman is credited, and Dawud is not diminished.

**Al-Hasan al-Basri and the weeping judge.** Ibn Abi Hatim records that when Iyas bin Muʿawiyah was appointed a judge, Al-Hasan came to him and found him weeping. Iyas said that of what he had heard about judges, one studies a case and his judgement is wrong, so he goes to Hell; another is biased by his own whims and desires, so he goes to Hell; and another studies a case and gives the right judgement, so he goes to Paradise. Al-Hasan Al-Basari answered that what Allah tells us about Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them both) and the prophets and the judgements they made proves that what these people said is wrong — and he recited ayah 78, ending *"and We were witness to their judgement."* Then he said: "Allah praised Sulayman but He did not condemn Dawud." The sentence is Al-Hasan's reading of the ayah, not part of the ayah.

Al-Hasan then named three things Allah enjoins on judges: not to sell their office for a miserable price, not to follow their own whims and desires, and not to fear anyone concerning their judgements. He recited for each: *"O Dawud! Verily, We have placed you as a successor on the earth; so judge between men in truth and follow not your desire"* (38:26), *"fear not men but fear Me"* and *"sell not My Ayat for a miserable price"* (5:44).

Ibn Kathir adds: the prophets were all infallible and supported by Allah; as for everyone else, it is recorded in **Sahih Al-Bukhari** from ʿAmir bin Al-ʿAs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"If the judge does his best, studies the case and reaches the right conclusion, he will have two rewards. If he does his best, studies the case and reaches the wrong conclusion, he will have one reward."* This hadith, says Ibn Kathir, refutes what Iyas feared.

## The wolf and the two women

Ibn Kathir cites a similar story recorded by **Imam Ahmad in his Musnad** from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: two women each had a son; a wolf came and took one of the children; they brought their dispute to Dawud, who ruled the remaining child belonged to the older woman. As they left, Sulayman called them and said, "Give me a sword and I will divide him between the two of you." The younger woman said, "May Allah have mercy on you! He is her child, do not cut him up!" So he ruled the child was hers. Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by **Al-Bukhari and Muslim** in their Sahihs, and that **An-Nasa'i** devoted a chapter to it in the Book of Judgements.

The same instinct twice: Sulayman looks past the claim to the thing itself — a vine that can regrow, a child who must not be cut — and finds the ruling that saves it.

## What the jurists took from this passage

**Can a judge reverse his own verdict?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarises Qurtubi's long discussion. A verdict conflicting with the sacred law is invalid by consensus of the Ummah, and another judge must nullify it, rule correctly, and remove the incompetent judge. But a verdict grounded in the law and in *ijtihad* — a qualified scholar's disciplined reasoning to reach a ruling — may not be overturned by another judge, or the whole judicial order collapses. If the judge himself later realises his own reasoning was mistaken, he may — and preferably should — change it. In his detailed letter to Abu Musa al-Ashʿari on the principles of judging, ʿUmar wrote that if one's ijtihad changes after judgement, the judgement should change to match (reported by Dar Qutni).

**Or was it never a reversal?** Mujahid held that both judgements were sound in their own right: Dawud's was strictly judicial, Sulayman's in the nature of a compromise between the parties — and the Qur'an says *wa'l-sulhu khayr*, "and compromise is better" (4:128). That, on this view, is why Allah praised the second (Mazhari); and no verdict was revoked at all, since a compromise was willingly agreed between the parties before they left the court. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ʿUmar instructed his judges to attempt a settlement first and rule by jurisprudence only if none was possible — because the loser in a judgement has no option but to accept it, yet develops hostility in his heart towards his rival, whereas a compromise removes the ill will.

**When two qualified scholars disagree, is only one right?** Those holding that conflicting verdicts can both be valid point to *"and to each of them We gave wisdom and knowledge"* — no admonition of Dawud, no warning of error. Those holding that only one can be correct point to *"We made Sulayman understand it"* — the right answer was disclosed to one of them, so the other's, though free of blame, was not it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that since the Prophet ﷺ taught that a scholar whose ijtihad is correct has two rewards while one who errs still has one, the difference between the two schools is largely one of terms: on the first view the erring scholar's ijtihad is valid and acting on it brings salvation; on the second his reward is simply less — and either way he is free from blame and his followers are not sinners.

**Livestock that damage a neighbour's land.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cautions that a ruling given in the legal code of Dawud does not automatically carry into the Shariʿah of the Prophet ﷺ, which is why the cardinal jurists differ. Imam Shafiʿi held the owner liable for damage done at night but not by day — basing it in fact not on this story but on a *mursal* report (one with a gap at the end of its chain) in the **Muwatta' of Imam Malik**, about a camel of Baraʼ Ibn ʿAzib that entered someone's orchard and damaged it: the Prophet ﷺ ruled that guarding fields and orchards by night is the owners' responsibility, but if the animals damaged the crop despite reasonable measures, the animals' owner compensates. Imam Abu Hanifah and the jurists of the Kufa school held instead that liability turns on negligence: if the owner or shepherd is with the animals and they damage a field through his carelessness, he compensates by day or night; if an unattended animal strays with no negligence on his part, he does not, whatever the hour — citing the hadith *jubar jurh al-ʿajmaʼ*, that the wound caused by an animal is not compensated, reported by **Bukhari and Muslim**.

## Mountains and birds (ayah 79)

*"And We subjected the mountains and the birds to glorify Our praises along with Dawud. And it was We Who were the doer."*

Ibn Kathir explains this by the beauty of his voice when he recited his Book, Az-Zabur: when he recited it beautifully the birds would stop and hover in the air and repeat after him, and the mountains would respond and echo his words.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān separates two things: the melodious voice was an outward excellence Allah granted him, while the joining of birds and mountains in praise was a *miracle* — and for a miracle it is not necessary that these things already possessed life and intelligence, since a miracle can give understanding to what did not have it before.

Ibn Kathir then records that the Prophet ﷺ passed by Abu Musa Al-Ashʿari reciting Qur'an at night in a very beautiful voice, stopped and listened, and said that this man had been given one of the beautiful voices of the family of Dawud. Abu Musa said, "O Messenger of Allah, if I had known you were listening, I would have done my best for you."

## The armour, and the question at the end (ayah 80)

*"And We taught him the making of metal coats of mail, to protect you in your fighting. Are you then grateful?"*

**The word.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *labus* lexically covers what is worn for protection; here it means the armour worn in battle against an enemy. Ibn Kathir specifies the manufacture of chain-armour, and Qatadah said that before this people used to wear plated armour — Dawud was the first to make rings of chain-armour. Elsewhere the Qur'an says *"And We made the iron soft for him… Make perfect coats of mail, and balance well the rings"* (34:10–11), which Ibn Kathir glosses as the craftsman's exact tolerance: not so loose that the rings shake, not so tight that they cannot move at all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions two ways the softening of iron is understood: that it became soft like wax in his hands, or that he was taught to heat it until it could be moulded, as foundries do today.

**Who the gift was for.** The ayah does not say "to protect *him*." It says *"to protect **you**"* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, in your battles. *"Are you then grateful?"* — that is, Allah blessed you when He inspired His servant Dawud and taught him this for your sake.

**Living it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion out: protection in combat is a need felt universally, for religious and worldly purposes alike, and Allah presents the skill of meeting it as something He taught a prophet — so learning and teaching any skill that serves people's needs is an act of virtue, provided it is meant for their good and not merely for monetary gain. Different prophets were engaged in different skills; Adam used his skill in farming. The Prophet ﷺ said that a producer who makes his product intending to serve people is like the mother of Musa, who fed her own child and was paid for her services too — drawing double benefit.

## The wind (ayah 81)

*"And to Sulayman the wind, strongly raging, running by his command towards the land which We had blessed."*

**One letter carries a whole distinction.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out (citing Ruh ul-Maʿani, with reference to Al-Baydawi) that this sentence continues *"And with Dawud We subjugated…"* in ayah 79 — but the wording shifts. With Dawud the Qur'an uses *maʿa*, "with": the birds and hills glorified Allah alongside him, simultaneously, without any command from him. With Sulayman it uses the letter *lam*, "for": the wind acted according to his commands, carrying him where and when he desired.

**A raging wind that harmed nothing.** *ʿAsifah* literally means a strong, violent wind — yet elsewhere the Qur'an describes it blowing *rukhaʼan*, gently, by his order wherever he willed (38:36), while covering a month's journey by morning and a month by afternoon (34:12). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles these: in itself it was strong enough to accomplish two months' journey in one day, yet it created no turbulence; it is reported that when the platform flew, no birds were harmed by the velocity of the wind.

**The blessed land** it runs toward is Ash-Sham, Greater Syria (Ibn Kathir).

**The travelling court.** Ibn Kathir describes a mat made of wood on which Sulayman would place all the equipment of his kingship — horses, camels, tents and troops — and command the wind to carry it, going underneath it while it carried him aloft, until it reached wherever he wanted and set everything down. Ibn Abi Hatim narrates on the authority of Saʿid Ibn Jubair that six hundred thousand chairs were placed on this platform: believing humans in front with Sulayman, believing jinn behind them, and the birds commanded to fly above and shield it from the heat of the sun. Some traditions report that throughout the flight he sat with his head bowed, praying to and thanking Allah in all humility, not turning his head right or left.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relates from Hasan al-Basri that Sulayman once missed the ʿAsr prayer, so absorbed was he in inspecting his cavalry horses, and in his regret removed those horses from service; because the act was done to win Allah's goodwill, Allah rewarded him by making the wind subservient to him — a superior and faster conveyance.

And the ayah signs off: *"And of everything We are the All-Knower."*

## The jinn (ayah 82)

*"And of the Shayatin were some who dived for him, and did other work besides that; and it was We Who guarded them."*

Ibn Kathir: they dived into the water to retrieve pearls and jewels for him, and did other work besides — as elsewhere, *"every kind of builder and diver, and others bound in fetters"* (38:37–38), and *"fashioning for him whatsoever he would — places of worship, statues, basins like water-troughs"* (34:13). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that he also put them to hard labour on different projects.

**Who exactly is meant.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: these are ethereal beings made of fire, possessing intelligence and understanding and obligated to follow the sacred law as humans are; beings that meet this description are called *jinn*, while those among them who disobey the law and persist in unbelief are called *shayatin*. All the jinn were made subservient to Sulayman, believers and unbelievers alike — but the believers regarded obeying him as a religious duty even before being formally placed under his command, so there was no need to mention them; the reference here is to the *rebellious* ones.

**"And it was We Who were guarding them."** Ibn Kathir: Allah protected him so that none of these shayatin could do him any harm. They were all subject to his control and domination, none of them would have dared approach him, and he could set free or detain whichever of them he wished. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān suggests this is perhaps why it was added at all: Sulayman was exposed to danger from the unbelieving jinn. The protection is credited to Allah, not to his own command over them.

## What the whole passage is saying

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with an observation from Razi. To Dawud, Allah made subservient things that are extremely hard and dense — iron and mountains. To Sulayman, things that are ethereal and cannot even be perceived — wind and jinn. Between them, this shows that He is omnipotent and that His authority extends over all created things.

So we are given a judge who accepted a better answer from his own son, a craftsman-king whose invention is presented to us as a favour we owe thanks for, and a ruler of wind and jinn who flew with his head bowed. Every gift named here carries its Giver's name — *We taught, We subjected, We were guarding* — and the one response the passage explicitly asks for is in ayah 80: *"Are you then grateful?"*

passages.title: Job's patience and the steadfast prophets
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat give us the prophet remembered above all others for patience — Ayyub (Job) — and then three more names sealed with the same quality. What holds the passage together is one word: **ṣabr**, steadfast endurance. Ayah 83 shows what such endurance sounds like when it finally speaks; ayah 84 shows what Allah does in response; ayat 85–86 widen the frame, so that Ayyub is one of a company of servants who held firm and were brought into Allah's mercy.

## The trial of Ayyub

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us here about Ayyub and the trials that struck him in three areas at once: **his wealth, his children and his physical health.** He had plenty of livestock, cattle and crops, many children and beautiful houses — and he was tested in all of it until he had lost everything he owned. Then he was tested with regard to his body. He was left alone at the edge of the city, and there was no one who treated him with compassion apart from his wife, who took care of him. Ibn Kathir adds that it was said this reached the stage where she herself was in need, so she began to serve people, to earn something for his sake.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture from Ibn Kathir's account: Allah had given Ayyub, in his early life, every sort of material comfort — wealth, property, magnificent houses, children, servants and attendants — and then he faced the kind of trial by which prophets are tested, and was deprived of all of it. On top of that came a serious disease, like leprosy, which affected his whole body **except the heart and the tongue** — and in that miserable condition he spent his time in prayer and in giving thanks to Allah with his heart and his tongue. Everything that could be taken from him was taken; what remained was exactly what worship requires — a heart that remembers and a tongue that praises.

Because of this illness his relatives, friends and neighbours avoided him and placed him near a garbage dump outside the city. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, on Ibn Kathir's authority, that his wife was either the daughter or the granddaughter of Yūsuf (peace be upon him), named Layyā daughter of Mīshā ibn Yūsuf. With all his wealth gone, she worked and earned a living for them both and nursed him through his illness.

**An honest word about the details.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say that the story of Ayyub is based mostly on Jewish legends, and that it reproduces only those elements which scholars of hadith consider historically reliable. What the Qur'an itself tells us, it says, is only this: he suffered from some serious disease and endured it with fortitude; ultimately he prayed to Allah for recovery and it was granted; during his illness his family members and friends disappeared, either dying or abandoning him to his fate; then Allah restored him to complete health and gave him back all his children and an equal number in addition. Hold the outline firmly; hold the embellishments lightly.

## Why the best are tested hardest

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the framing: the ordeal of Ayyub "was nothing new, nor something to be wondered at." It then cites the Prophet ﷺ as having said that **the prophets face the most severe tests, and then come the other believers according to their degree of piety**; and, in another tradition, that every man is tested according to his adherence and devotion to religion — the stronger his beliefs, the harder the test to which he is subjected, so that his rewards are in proportion to his sufferings.

Ibn Kathir cites the same two sayings of the Prophet ﷺ: that **the people who are tested most severely are the Prophets, then the righteous, then the next best and the next best**; and that a man will be tested according to his level of religious commitment — the stronger his religious commitment, the more severe will be his test. Severity of trial, on this reckoning, is not a sign of Allah's displeasure; in the lives of the Prophets it tracked closeness to Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also places Ayyub in a pairing worth remembering: he occupies a distinctive position among all the prophets for firmness in devotion and endurance in suffering **in the same manner as Dāwūd (peace be upon him) enjoyed distinction for offering thanks to Allah.**

## What he said when he had nothing

Ibn Kathir records from Yazīd ibn Maysarah — the report is in Ibn Abī Ḥātim — that when Allah tested Ayyub with the loss of his family, wealth and children, and he had nothing left, he began to focus upon the remembrance of Allah and said: he praised the Lord of lords, who had bestowed His kindness upon him and given him wealth and children, and confessed that there had been no corner of his heart that was not filled with attachment to those worldly things; then Allah took all of that away and emptied his heart, "and there is nothing to stand between me and You." He added that if his enemy Iblīs knew of this, he would be jealous of him — and when Iblīs heard of it, he became upset. Ayyub also said: O Lord, You gave me wealth and children, and there was no one standing at my door complaining of some wrong I had done to him — You know that. And: I used to have a bed prepared for me, but I forsook it and said to myself, you were not created to lie on a comfortable bed; I forsook it only for Your sake.

## The words of ayah 83 — a prayer that is not a complaint

In ayah 83 he says only **«مَسَّنِيَ الضُّرُّ»** — "distress has seized me" — and then **«وَأَنتَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ»**, "and You are the Most Merciful of all those who show mercy." He names his condition and he names his Lord's attribute. He does not itemise his losses, and he does not phrase a demand.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes a whole section to this, under the heading that **his invocation is not counter to patience.** He spent seven years and some months lying near that garbage dump outside the city, but never once did he lose heart, nor did he ever utter a word of complaint about his fate. His wife Layyā once asked him to pray to Allah for His mercy, as his sufferings had become unbearable. He replied that, having enjoyed seventy years of the best of health surrounded by all the luxuries money could buy, it would be unworthy of him to complain because a mere seven years had been spent in pain and poverty. His firm prophetic resolve, self-discipline and fortitude prevented him from beseeching Allah's mercy on his condition, lest it be construed as an act contrary to unquestioning submission to the will of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds the crucial clarification: **to invoke Allah's mercy for relief from suffering does not mean absence of fortitude.** Ultimately something happened which made him pray to Allah for His mercy — but this was just a prayer and did not express a sense of complaint. And the proof that it cost him nothing of his rank is that Allah has put His seal in acknowledgement of his extreme endurance in another surah: **«إِنَّا وَجَدْنَاهُ صَابِرًا»** — "Surely We found him a steadfast man" (38:44). For anyone carrying illness or loss, this is the practical centre of the passage: his prayer was a prayer, not a grievance — and Allah still called him steadfast.

## Ayah 84: the answer, and what "the like of them" means

The response comes with no gap at all: **«فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ فَكَشَفْنَا مَا بِهِ مِن ضُرٍّ»** — "So We answered his call, and We removed the distress that was on him." The very word he had used of himself, *ḍurr*, is the word used for what Allah lifted off him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, how the cure came: when his supplication was granted, he was told to **rub his heels on the ground**, and a stream of fresh and clear water would gush forth; he should bathe himself in it and also drink it, and the disease would disappear. He did as he was told, and in no time his body — covered with boils and reduced to skin and bones — regained its original shape and health. Allah sent him garments from Paradise, which he wore, and he sat down in a corner away from the garbage dump. His wife came to see him as usual and, not finding him, began to cry. She did not recognise him sitting nearby, because his appearance had changed completely; she asked this stranger whether he had any information about the sick man who used to lie there. When Ayyub revealed himself, she still did not believe him until he informed her that Allah had healed his body after he invoked His mercy. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that after this, Allah restored to him all his wealth and children, and gave him more children equal in number to those he had before.

Ibn Kathir also records, from Ibn Abī Ḥātim on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah healed Ayyub He sent upon him a shower of **golden locusts**, and Ayyub began picking them up and gathering them in his garment. It was said to him, "O Ayyub, have you not had enough?" He said: **"O Lord, who can ever have enough of Your mercy?"** Ibn Kathir notes that the basis of this hadith is recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. After all that stripping away, what he could not have his fill of was not wealth but mercy.

**«وَآتَيْنَاهُ أَهْلَهُ وَمِثْلَهُم مَّعَهُمْ»** — "and We restored his family to him, and the like thereof along with them." Ibn Kathir gathers the views. It was reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said, **"They themselves were restored to him"** — also narrated from him by al-ʿAwfī; something similar was narrated from Ibn Masʿūd and Mujāhid, and this was the view of al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. Mujāhid transmits a striking version: it was said to Ayyub, "Your family will be with you in Paradise; if you want, We will bring them back to you, or if you want, We will leave them for you in Paradise and will compensate you with others like them." He said, "No, leave them for me in Paradise." So they were left for him in Paradise, and he was compensated with others like them in this world.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds Ibn Masʿūd's report that Ayyub had seven sons and seven daughters, all of whom died while he was undergoing the ordeal; when his days of hardship were over, Allah brought his children back to life and his wife also gave birth to as many more — this being what "and the like thereof along with them" refers to. According to al-Thaʿlabī this version is closer to the text of the Qur'an (reported via al-Qurṭubī). Some scholars say instead that he was granted as many new children as he had before, and that *mithl*, "the like," refers to an equal number of **grandchildren**. The commentators leave it there: *only Allah knows best.* The Qur'an's certainty is that the loss was more than made good; the mechanism is where the scholars differed.

## "A mercy from Ourselves, and a Reminder for all those who worship Us"

Ayah 84 ends by naming two purposes. **«رَحْمَةً مِّنْ عِندِنَا»** — "as a mercy from Ourselves": Ibn Kathir says simply that Allah did that for him as a mercy from Allah towards him.

**«وَذِكْرَىٰ لِلْعَابِدِينَ»** — "and a Reminder for all those who worship Us." Here Ibn Kathir gives the passage its purpose for us: Allah made Ayyub **an example, lest those who are beset by trials think that He does that to them because He does not care for them** — so that they may take him as an example of patience in accepting the decrees of Allah and bearing the trials with which He tests His servants as He wills. "And Allah has the utmost wisdom with regard to that." On Ibn Kathir's reading the story is preserved not as biography but against a specific, corrosive thought that comes to every suffering believer: *I have been abandoned.*

## Ayat 85–86: Ismāʿīl, Idrīs and Dhu'l-Kifl

Ayah 85 names three more and closes them with **«كُلٌّ مِّنَ الصَّابِرِينَ»** — "all were from among the patient." Ibn Kathir notes that Ismāʿīl was the son of Ibrāhīm al-Khalīl, peace be upon them both, and that he has already been mentioned in Sūrat Maryam, where mention was also made of Idrīs.

**Was Dhu'l-Kifl a prophet?** Ibn Kathir's judgement is that from the context, and from his being mentioned alongside Prophets, it appears that he was also a Prophet. Others say he was a righteous man, a just king and a fair judge. **Ibn Jarīr refrained from making any decisive comment** — "and Allah knows best." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents the same disagreement: about Ismāʿīl and Idrīs there is no doubt, since the Qur'an names them as prophets several times, but on Dhu'l-Kifl some other versions do not include him among the prophets, saying rather that he was a saint or a pious person. It is right to leave it as the scholars left it.

**The story behind the name.** Ibn Jarīr reports on the authority of Mujāhid that when the prophet al-Yasaʿ grew old and weak, he thought of appointing someone to perform a prophet's duties on his behalf during his lifetime. He assembled his companions and set three conditions for the deputy: that he fast all the year round, spend his nights in prayer, and never lose his temper. A relatively unknown man, held in contempt by the people, stood up and offered himself, affirming all three conditions. Al-Yasaʿ perhaps did not believe his claim and rejected him. After a few days he reconvened the meeting and repeated the conditions; everyone remained seated except the same man, who stood again — and this time he was appointed deputy.

When Iblīs realised this, he sent his aides to entice Dhu'l-Kifl into something that would cost him the post; all of them excused themselves, saying he was beyond their power to harm. So Iblīs said, "Alright, leave him to me." Dhu'l-Kifl fasted by day and prayed the whole night, taking only a little nap in the afternoon. Iblīs came just as the nap was due, claiming to be an old, tortured man, and spun out a long tale of the cruelty and injustice he had suffered until no time was left for the nap; Dhu'l-Kifl told him to come to his court and he would see justice done — and the man never appeared. The next day the same thing happened, with the excuse that his opponents had agreed to settle out of court and then gone back on their promise. On the third day, worn out from two days without sleep, Dhu'l-Kifl asked his household to let no one knock at the door. The old man came, was stopped by the family, entered through a ventilator, and knocked at the door of his room. Seeing that the man had come inside while the door was still closed, Dhu'l-Kifl asked how — and then realised who he was: "Are you Allah's enemy Iblīs?" He admitted it and said that all his plans had been thwarted; his intention had been to make him angry somehow, so that one of his claims before al-Yasaʿ could be proved false. It was because of this episode, the report says, that he was given the title **Dhu'l-Kifl**, meaning one who is true to his covenant and performs his duties faithfully. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Kathir.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also mentions a separate narrative quoted in the *Musnad* of Aḥmad, reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar, about a great sinner among the Children of Israel named **Kifl** who was forgiven after turning back from a sin out of pity for a woman driven to it by her circumstances. Ibn Kathir observed, after quoting it, that none of the six authentic books of hadith reports this tradition and its authority is weak — and that even if the tradition is true, the name in it is *Kifl*, not *Dhu'l-Kifl*, which means it concerns a different man. It is noted here only because the two names are often confused; it should not be read into ayah 85.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own summary is measured: Dhu'l-Kifl was the deputy of the prophet al-Yasaʿ, and it is possible that his name is mentioned along with prophets because of his virtuous deeds; it is equally possible that he was initially the deputy and was later elevated by Allah to the status of a prophet.

## Ayah 86: where patience ends up

**«وَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ فِي رَحْمَتِنَا إِنَّهُم مِّنَ الصَّالِحِينَ»** — "And We admitted them to Our mercy. Verily, they were of the righteous."

**A reflection on the shape of the passage** — a reader's observation, not a point drawn from the commentaries. Ayah 83 is a servant's voice appealing to Allah as **the Most Merciful of all those who show mercy**; ayah 86 ends with Allah **admitting** these servants into His mercy. And notice the two descriptions that bracket them: in ayah 85 they are *from among the patient*, in ayah 86 *of the righteous*. Ayyub's spared heart and tongue — praying and giving thanks beside a garbage dump, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes him — is what such patience looked like in practice.

**Living it.** Three things this passage asks of a believer. First, that when trial comes, you do not read it as evidence that Allah has stopped caring for you — Ibn Kathir says Ayyub was made an example precisely against that thought. Second, that you keep whatever worship remains possible, even if all that is left working is a heart and a tongue. Third, that you call on Allah plainly, naming your need and naming His mercy, without treating the asking as a failure of patience — for as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, invoking Allah's mercy for relief from suffering does not mean an absence of fortitude. Allah answered a man who did all three, removed his distress, restored what he had lost and more, and then placed his name in the same list as Ismāʿīl, Idrīs and Dhu'l-Kifl.

passages.title: Jonah's prayer from the darkness
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat tell the story of the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), peace be upon him — a messenger who walked away from his people, ended up in the belly of a fish at the bottom of the sea, and called out to Allah from inside layers of darkness. What holds them together is a single movement: ayah 87 takes him down into the darkness and gives us the words he said there; ayah 88 lifts him out and then, in its closing clause, hands that same rescue to every believer who calls on Allah the way he did. The passage is not primarily about a fish. It is about what a servant says when everything else has been taken away, and what Allah does in response.

## The story behind the ayah

Ibn Kathir gives the background. Yunus ibn Matta, upon him be peace, was sent by Allah to the people of Nineveh, a town in the area of Mawsil in northern Iraq. He called them to Allah; they rejected him and persisted in their disbelief. So he left them in anger, threatening them with punishment after three days.

Then his people realised that he was telling the truth — and that a Prophet never lies. They went out to the desert with their children and their cattle and flocks. They separated the mothers from their young, then beseeched Allah and pleaded with Him: the camels and their young groaning, the cows and their calves mooing, the sheep and their lambs bleating. So Allah spared them from the punishment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that they repented and asked pardon for their sins, and that according to some versions they had actually seen the signs of the impending disaster; Allah accepted their sincere contrition and released them from the fear of it. This is the town the Qur'an singles out elsewhere: "Was there any town that believed (after seeing the punishment), and its faith saved it? Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the torment of disgrace in the life of the world, and permitted them to enjoy for a while" (10:98).

Yunus, meanwhile, was waiting for news of the destruction of his people. When he learnt that the storm had passed and his people were safe and sound, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, he worried that they would regard him as a liar. According to some versions, it was customary with his people to execute a person proved a liar (Mazhari); so he feared for his life and decided to go away to some other place rather than return to them.

He came to water and boarded a boat. Ibn Kathir says he travelled with some people on a ship which was tossed about on the sea; the people feared they would drown, so they cast lots to choose a man to throw overboard. The lot fell to Yunus — and they refused to throw him overboard. This happened a second and a third time. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the boatmen seem to have been aware of his exalted position, which is why they refused. This is what the Qur'an means in "Then he ˹agreed to˺ cast lots, and he was among the losers" (37:141) — the draw went against him. Yunus then stood up, removed his garment, and cast himself into the sea.

And a fish was already on its way. According to what Ibn Masʿud said, Allah sent it from the Green Sea (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reporting the same narration from Ibn Masʿud, says the fish came from the Caspian Sea) — a large fish which cleaved the oceans until it came and swallowed Yunus as he threw himself in. Allah inspired that large fish not to devour his flesh or break his bones. Ibn Kathir renders the instruction unforgettably: as if He said, *Yunus is not food for you — rather your belly is a prison for him.*

Read that sentence slowly. The very creature that looks like the end of him is under orders. It is not a predator; it is a cell. Every wall of Yunus's confinement was placed there by the One he was about to call upon.

## What exactly was the lapse?

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does its most careful work, and it deserves attention, because Ahl al-Sunnah hold the prophets in the highest honour and we must not read into the passage more fault than the scholars found.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that there are references in the Qur'an that Yunus, peace be upon him, earned Allah's displeasure when he left his people without His specific command, and that his stay for a few days in the stomach of the fish was a sign of that displeasure. But displeasure at what, precisely? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reasons step by step: it is safe to assume that his warning of destruction within three days was not the outcome of his own judgement but based on Divine revelation. Similarly, his dissociation from his people was nothing new and was in line with the practice of other prophets in similar situations, and must therefore also have been done by the command and approval of Allah. **Up to that point there seems nothing to be wrong in his conduct which would deserve Allah's displeasure.**

The turn comes afterwards. When Allah accepted the genuine remorse and repentance of the people and released them from the fear of destruction, it was to be expected that Yunus would return to them. His decision not to return was based on his own judgement — *ijtihād*, a considered personal judgement — and his reasons were sound ones: they would regard him as a liar, his teachings would be rendered ineffectual and fruitless, and there was the danger that he might be taken and executed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that this did not constitute a sin. Nevertheless, for a prophet to take a decision on his own without waiting for the revelation (*waḥy*) from Allah was not liked by Him. This was not a crime, but an act which was not desirable. The status of the prophets and of those close to Allah is so highly exalted that it is expected of them not to indulge even in such undesirable acts; the slightest lapse on their part is subjected to Allah's displeasure and reproach — and that, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is why he faced this hardship.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also quotes Tafsir al-Qurtubi, from al-Qushairi, that this happened to Yunus when the tempest was removed from his people against his wish, and that his stay in the stomach of the fish for a few days was **more of a reformatory measure than a punishment** — as sometimes people warn their young children and take corrective measures with them.

## The words themselves

**Dhun-Nūn — "the man of the fish."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an mentions him in some places by his real name, Yunus, and in others by the title *Dhunnun* or *Sahib Al-Hut*. The meaning of *Nun* and *Hut* is both "fish"; so both titles can be translated "man of the fish." He is referred to this way, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, because of the episode in which he remained inside the stomach of a fish for a few days, in very odd circumstances, by the will of Allah. Ibn Kathir confirms that *Nun* here refers to the fish, and that it is correct for it to be attributed to him. It is worth pausing on that — and here I am reflecting rather than quoting: Allah names him, in this very ayah, by the hardest passage of his life, and the place of his confinement became part of how he is honoured in the Book.

**"When he went off in anger" (*idh dhahaba mughāḍiban*).** Whose anger, and at whom? Ibn Kathir reports that Ad-Dahhak said: "Anger towards his people." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says it is obvious that the anger was against his own people, and that Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, explained it as such.

**"And imagined that We shall not punish him" (*fa-ẓanna an lan naqdira ʿalayh*).** This is the phrase in ayah 87 that most needs care, and the sources give it real attention. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three lexical possibilities for *naqdira*:

1. That it carries the sense of power — that Yunus imagined Allah would not be able to gain mastery over him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls this obviously an unacceptable explanation: no Muslim can ever entertain such thoughts in his mind, least of all a prophet of Allah.
2. From *qadr*, meaning to straiten or narrow down — as the Qur'an says, "Allah extends provision to whom He wills and straitens it." On this reading, Yunus thought that he would not be put in a straitened condition by Allah if he abandoned his people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names the imams of tafsir ʿAta', Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Hasan Basri and many other scholars for this view, and says this explanation is adopted by most commentators. Ibn Kathir carries the same sense — "constrict him in the belly of the fish" — reporting something similar from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak and others, and noting that this was the view favoured by Ibn Jarir, who quoted as evidence the ayah: "and the man whose resources are restricted, let him spend according to what Allah has given him. Allah puts no burden on any person beyond what He has given him. Allah will grant after hardship, ease" (65:7).
3. From *taqdīr*, decree or determination — in which case the verse would mean that Yunus was sure he would not be blamed if he dissociated himself from his people. Qatadah, Mujahid and Farra' have adopted this explanation.

So the two readings the scholars work with both keep the meaning within the bounds of a prophet's certainty about his Lord: he did not expect to be straitened, or he did not expect to be blamed. Where the scholars differ, take both as they stand — the sources present them side by side, not as one settled and one rejected.

**"The darknesses" (*aẓ-ẓulumāt*), plural.** Ibn Masʿud said of the depths of darkness: "The darkness of the belly of the fish, the darkness of the sea and the darkness of the night." Ibn Kathir reports this also from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan and Qatadah. Salim ibn Abu al-Jaʿd said: "The darkness of the fish in the belly of another fish in the darkness of the sea." Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas and others said that the fish took him through the sea, cleaving it until it reached the bottom of the sea — and there Yunus heard the rocks at the bottom of the sea uttering glorification of Allah, at which point he said his prayer.

That detail is the hinge of the whole passage. In the most silent, sealed, hopeless-looking place in creation, the stones were already busy glorifying Allah. Yunus, hearing them, joined in.

Ibn Kathir also records from ʿAwf al-Aʿrabi: "When Yunus found himself in the belly of the fish, he thought that he had died. Then he moved his legs. When he moved his legs, he prostrated where he was, then he called out: 'O Lord, I have taken a place of worship to You in a place which no other person has reached.'"

## The prayer

**لَّا إِلَـٰهَ إِلَّا أَنتَ سُبْحَانَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ الظَّالِمِينَ**
*"There is no god but You, Glorified be You! Truly, I have been of the wrongdoers."*

Notice its shape. It contains no request. Yunus does not ask to be let out. He begins with *tawḥīd* — there is no god but You. He follows with *tasbīḥ* — glorifying Allah, declaring Him free of any fault. And he ends with confession: truly, I have been of the wrongdoers. Affirm your Lord, glorify Him, take the blame yourself — and the rescue in ayah 88 comes without his ever having named what he wanted.

## Ayah 88: the rescue, and the promise

"So We answered his call, and delivered him from the distress." Ibn Kathir explains this as: We brought him forth from the belly of the fish and from that darkness. The grief and the confinement are lifted together.

Then the clause that turns a story into a doorway: **"And thus We do deliver the believers."** Ibn Kathir explains: this means when they are in difficulty and they call upon Allah and repent to Him, especially if they call upon Him with these words at the time of distress. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same: just as He released Yunus from his misery and distress, so does He deliver other believers when they turn towards Him repenting their sins sincerely. The rescue is not a one-off miracle for a prophet; it is how Allah deals with anyone who returns to Him.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir notes that the leader of the Prophets ﷺ encouraged us to call upon Allah with these words, and records a striking incident. Imam Ahmad recorded that Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, said that he passed ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, in the Masjid and greeted him; ʿUthman stared at him but did not return the Salam. Saʿd went to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and said, "O Commander of the faithful, has something happened in Islam?" ʿUmar sent for ʿUthman and asked him why he had not returned his brother's Salam. ʿUthman at first denied it, and it reached the point where they both swore oaths. Then ʿUthman remembered and said: "Yes, you are right, I seek the forgiveness of Allah and I repent to Him. You passed by me a short while ago but I was preoccupied with thoughts of something I had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which I never think of but a veil comes down over my eyes and my heart."

Saʿd then told him what it was. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had told them the first part of a supplication when a bedouin came and kept him busy; then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up and Saʿd followed him, and when he grew worried that he would enter his house, he stamped his feet. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned and said, "Who is this? Abu Ishaq?" — "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." — "What is the matter?" Saʿd said, "Nothing, by Allah, except that you told us the first part of the supplication, then this bedouin came and kept you busy." He said:

> "Yes — the supplication of Dhun-Nun when he was in the belly of the fish: *Lā ilāha illā anta, subḥānaka, innī kuntu min aẓ-ẓālimīn.* No Muslim ever prays to his Lord with these words for anything, but He will answer his prayer."

Ibn Kathir notes that it was also recorded by At-Tirmidhi, and by An-Nasa'i in *Al-Yawm wal-Laylah*. He further reports that Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Saʿd said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever offers supplication in the words of the supplication of Yunus, will be answered" — and Abu Saʿid said that he was referring to the closing words of ayah 88, "And thus We do deliver the believers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān conveys the same teaching as a hadith of the Holy Prophet ﷺ, citing it as "(Ahmad, Tirmidhi, Mahari)": if a Muslim prays to Allah for the grant of a wish in the words used by Yunus when he was in the stomach of the fish, He would accept his prayer and grant his wish.

## Living it

The points below are reflection on what the sources above say, offered as ways to carry the passage into an ordinary week.

**Memorise the words and mean them.** The Prophet ﷺ did not merely tell the story; he handed us the sentence. It is short enough for a child and heavy enough for the worst night of your life. And note the scope in the wording reported by Ibn Kathir: no Muslim prays with these words "for anything" but He answers.

**Start where Yunus started.** The instinct in a crisis is to lead with the request. This prayer leads with who Allah is, then glorifies Him, then owns the fault — and the answer follows. If you are in a difficulty partly of your own making, that order is the way back.

**No darkness is outside His hearing.** Layers of dark, the bottom of the sea, inside a living creature — and the call was answered. And note who else was there: rocks, glorifying Allah where no eye could see.

**Not every hardship means you are hated.** On the report Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes from al-Qurtubi from al-Qushairi, the days in the fish were more of a reformatory measure than a punishment — the way a parent corrects a child. If you are being squeezed, it may be that you are being taught.

**And the ending is the point of the telling.** Ayah 88 does not close with "and We saved Yunus." It closes with "and thus We do deliver the believers" — the door left open for you.

passages.title: Zachariah's plea and the sign of Mary
passages.tafsir:
Two answered prayers, placed side by side: an aged prophet who asks not to be left without an heir, and a woman who guarded her chastity, of whom the passage records no request at all. Ayat 89–90 give the story of Zakariyya and the birth of Yahya; ayah 91 gives the story of Maryam and the birth of ʿIsa. What holds them together is a single argument about the power of Allah — He answers, and He creates as He wills.

## Why these two stories, in this order

Ibn Kathir points out that the placement is deliberate. Allah "mentions the story of Zakariyya first, followed by the story of Maryam because the one is connected to the other." The first, he says, is "the story of a child being born to an old man of advanced years, from an old woman who had been barren and had never given birth when she was younger." The second "is even more wondrous, for in this case a child was born from a female without (the involvement of) a male."

So the two ayat build in a rising line. Nature is stretched in ayah 90; in ayah 91 it is set aside altogether. The reader who accepts the first has already conceded the principle on which the second rests.

Ibn Kathir also observes that this is not the first telling. Of Zakariyya's story he says it "has already been given in detail at the beginning of Surah Maryam and also in Surah ʿImran.
