Here an abbreviated version is given." And of both stories together he notes that they "also appear in Surah Āl-ʿImrān and in Surah Maryam."

That is worth holding on to as you read. This passage is not the full narrative; it is the narrative compressed to its point. What remains is: he called, We answered, and We made them a sign.

## Ayah 89 — a prayer said quietly

**"When he cried to his Lord."** Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean he called "in secret, hiding it from his people." The cry was raised to Allah, not staged for an audience. The one thing that most exposed his weakness — his childlessness in old age — he said only where Allah could hear.

**"Leave me not single."** Ibn Kathir glosses this: "with no child and no heir to stand among the people after me." Notice what he adds. The ache is not only the private ache of a man without a son. It is the ache of a prophet who looks at his community and sees no one who will stand in his place when he is gone. Ibn Kathir opens the passage by saying Zakariyya "asked Allah to grant him a son who would be a Prophet after him." The prayer is about the survival of a mission, not merely a bloodline.

**"Though You are the Best of the inheritors."** Here is the heart of the ayah, and both commentaries stop on it.

Ibn Kathir calls it "a supplication and form of praise befitting the topic" — that is, the praise is not decorative, it is matched to what is being asked for. Zakariyya is asking about inheritance, so he praises Allah precisely as the One who inherits. When every heir has died and every estate has changed hands, what remains belongs to Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the manners in it. Zakariyya wished for a son and heir and prayed for one, "But at the same time he made it clear that Allah is the best heir no matter if he had a son or not." The commentary calls this "the manifestation of the prophetic respect": the prophets' "main concern... should always be toward Allah Taʿālā, and even if someone else came into focus, their attention should not deviate from the main objective."

That is a demanding standard, and a liberating one. Zakariyya asks with real longing — he does not pretend he is above wanting a child. But in the same breath he names Allah as the One who remains, whatever the answer. He wants the gift without letting the gift displace the Giver. This is a model for every dua a believer makes: ask plainly for what you want, and in the same sentence let it be known that your heart is not held hostage to the answer.

## Ayah 90 — the answer, and the character behind it

**"So We answered his call, and We bestowed upon him Yahya, and cured his wife for him."**

The third clause is the quiet miracle. On "cured his wife for him," Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Saʿid bin Jubayr: "She was barren and never had a child, then she gave birth." Zakariyya had prayed about himself — *leave me not single*. The answer reached into a body he had not mentioned and repaired what he had not asked to be repaired. Allah's response to a dua is not limited to the words of the dua.

**Who they were.** The rest of the ayah shifts from the story to the people in it, describing them in three strokes — and the pronoun is plural, "they," not Zakariyya alone.

**"Verily, they used to hasten on to do good deeds."** Ibn Kathir explains "good deeds" here as "acts of worship and acts of obedience towards Allah." And notice the verb the ayah chooses: not merely that they did good, but that they *hastened* to it — the opposite of the believer who intends to obey, eventually.

**"And they used to call on Us with hope and fear."** Two states, both said of the same act: calling upon Allah.

Ath-Thawri explained it: "Hoping for that (reward) which is with Us and fearing that (punishment) which is with Us." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings. One is that "they call Allah Taʿālā both in comfort and distress" — they were not fair-weather servants who remember Allah only when something breaks. The other is that "during their prayers they remain suspended between hope and fear hoping that Allah would forgive their sins and fearing that their lapses may bring on them His displeasure." That image — suspended between the two, tilting to neither — is the balance the ayah is describing. Hope alone becomes presumption; fear alone becomes despair. The believer prays with both hands.

**"And they were Khashiʿin before Us."** *Khushuʿ* is the inner lowliness and awe of a servant standing before Allah. Ibn Kathir gathers an unusually wide set of early explanations here, and the range itself teaches something:

- ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it means "sincerely believing in that which was revealed by Allah."
- Mujahid: "Truly believing."
- Abu Al-ʿAliyah: "Fearing."
- Abu Sinan: "Khushuʿ means the fear which should never leave our hearts."
- Also reported from Mujahid: the *Khashiʿin* are "those who are humble."
- Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak: "The Khashiʿin are those who humble themselves before Allah."

Ibn Kathir's own verdict is that "all of these suggestions are close in meaning." He is not picking a winner, and neither should we. *Khushuʿ* is a single inner posture with several faces: it looks like sincere faith when you examine what a person believes, like fear when you examine what they feel, like lowliness when you examine how they carry themselves before Allah. Abu Sinan's phrase is the sharpest — a fear that "should never leave our hearts," not a spike of emotion in a moment of crisis but a settled condition of the soul.

Read the three descriptions in order and you have a complete servant: outward action that hastens ahead, inward states held in balance, and beneath both a heart bowed low. The ayah sets this portrait right beside the answered prayer.

## Ayah 91 — the one who guarded her chastity

The ayah does not name Maryam. It identifies her by a deed: "she who guarded her chastity." Ibn Kathir confirms the reference is to Maryam, peace be upon her, and links it to the parallel ayah in Surah At-Tahrim: "And Maryam, the daughter of ʿImran who guarded her chastity. And We breathed into it [her garment] through Our Ruh" (66:12) — the bracketed gloss is Ibn Kathir's, identifying what "it" refers to.

There is dignity in her being named by her chastity rather than by her name. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes her as "the pious lady who controlled her passions."

**"We breathed into her through Our Ruh."** The ayah attributes the act to Allah in the divine plural. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the means: it was "through Jibraʼil" that Allah "breathed His Spirit into her and she gave birth to a son." We affirm what the ayah says as it says it — that the breathing was from Allah, of *Our Ruh*, honoured by its attribution to Him — without imagining any likeness to creation, and without emptying the words of their meaning.

**"And We made her and her son a sign for the nations."** Ibn Kathir explains the sign: it is "evidence that Allah is able to do all things and that He creates whatever He wills; verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be' – and it is!" He connects it to the ayah in Surah Maryam, "And (We wish) to appoint him as a sign to mankind" (19:21).

Note carefully what the ayah makes a sign: *her and her son*. Not the child alone. The mother is inside the evidence, not merely the setting for it. And the sign is for the nations — not for her generation or her people alone, but for every people who would hear of it afterwards, including us.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the last step in the logic. Her son was "a symbol of Allah's Divine Power that He can cause babies to be born without a father, and also without both the parents as in the case of Sayyidna ʿAdam," peace be upon him. Put the cases in sequence and the argument is complete: a human from neither father nor mother (Adam), a human from a mother without a father (ʿIsa), a human from parents long past the age of children (Yahya), and the ordinary birth of everyone else. All of them are the same power at work. Only habit makes us call some of them miracles and the rest of them normal.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the ayah's immediate purpose: it "directs the Holy Prophet ﷺ to tell his people the story." These are not stories told for their own sake. They are handed to the Prophet ﷺ as evidence to put before people about what Allah is able to do.

## Living it

**Ask, and mean the praise you attach.** Zakariyya's dua in ayah 89 is short enough to memorise and complete enough to imitate: name the need honestly, then name Allah by the attribute that fits the need, and let that attribute steady you if the answer is no.

**Take your weakness to Allah before you take it to people.** He called "in secret, hiding it from his people," as Ibn Kathir says. Not everything that hurts needs an audience.

**Do not pray only when something has broken.** On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's first reading of the ayah, they called on Allah "both in comfort and distress."

**Hasten.** Ibn Kathir glosses hastening to good deeds as "acts of worship and acts of obedience towards Allah." The delay you keep granting yourself is the thing this ayah names.

**Answered prayer is not a reward for cleverness in asking.** Ayah 90 spends more words on who these people were than on what they received. The hastening, the hope and fear, the khushuʿ — that is the ground the answer grew in.

passages.title: One religion splintered into sects
passages.tafsir:
After a long procession of prophets and their stories, Allah gathers them all into a single sentence: they were never separate religions, but one religion carried by many messengers. Ayat 92–94 are the verdict on that whole gallery: **one Lord, one call to worship (92); one humanity that tore that call into pieces (93); and one final accounting in which no believing effort is lost (94).**

## Where we are in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that up to this point the sūrah has been telling the stories of the prophets, along with the principles — major and minor — that those stories carry. And the basic beliefs running through them are the same: the Oneness of Allah, prophethood, and the Day of Resurrection. These, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, are common to all the prophets and are the foundation of their invitation to people to follow the True Faith.

Ayat 92–94 state that foundation openly, after the sūrah has spent so long showing it to us in narrative form.

## Ayah 92: "This, your ummah, is one"

**إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أُمَّتُكُمۡ أُمَّةٗ وَٰحِدَةٗ** — "Truly, this, your Ummah is one."

The word *ummah* in ordinary usage means a community or a people, and the early authorities are careful to tell us what it means here. Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Qatādah, and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam** all explained it the same way: *"Your religion is one religion."*

That is a striking agreement among five of the great early commentators, and it points the meaning firmly in one direction. What is being called *one* here is not a nation of bodies. It is the *dīn* — what you believe and Whom you worship.

**Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** adds a second layer that turns the verse from a statement into an instruction. He said of this ayah: *"In this Ayah, Allah explains to them what they should avoid and what they should do."* And on the phrase itself he said: *"Meaning, your path is one path. Certainly this is your Sharīʿah (Divine Law) which I have clearly explained to you."*

So the ayah is not merely informing you that the religion is one; it is telling you to stay on it. It marks the road and warns you off the verges.

## "And I am your Lord, therefore worship Me"

**وَأَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمۡ فَٱعۡبُدُونِ** — the reason follows the claim immediately. The religion is one because the Lord is One. Where there is one Master, there can only be one service.

Ibn Kathir shows that the Qur'an uses this same construction elsewhere when addressing the messengers as a body: *"O (you) Messengers! Eat of the Ṭayyibāt (good things) and do righteous deeds…"* leading to *"And I am your Lord, so have Taqwā of Me"* (23:51–52). The same address to the messengers, sealed the same way: **I am your Lord.**

## One religion, many laws

Here Ibn Kathir raises the question a thoughtful reader will already be asking. If the religion of all the prophets was one, why did their laws differ?

He answers with a statement of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: **"We Prophets are brothers from different mothers, and our religion is one."**

Ibn Kathir then states the point plainly: *what is meant here is that they all worshipped Allah Alone with no partner or associate, although the Laws of each Messenger may have differed*, and he cites Allah's words: *"To each among you, We have prescribed a Law and a clear way"* (5:48).

This is worth holding onto, because it protects two truths at once. The creed — worship of Allah alone with no partner or associate — is one, undivided, and shared by every prophet. And the revealed laws genuinely did differ from one messenger to the next, which the Qur'an itself states without embarrassment. Brotherhood, not sameness.

*(Note: Ibn Kathir cites this statement of the Prophet ﷺ without naming a collection in this source, so we pass on the teaching without attaching it to a named book.)*

## Ayah 93: how the one road became many

**وَتَقَطَّعُوٓاْ أَمۡرَهُم بَيۡنَهُمۡ** — "But they have broken up and differed in their religion among themselves," rendered in the translation as: "Yet the people have divided it into sects."

The verb here carries the sense of breaking into pieces, and its object is *amrahum* — "their affair," their matter, the one thing that had been handed to them whole. The picture is of a single fabric torn up and the shreds distributed *baynahum*, "among themselves," each faction walking off with a scrap.

And notice the shift. Ayah 92 is addressed to the prophets: *your* religion is one. Ayah 93 speaks of the people in the third person: *they* divided it. The unity comes from Allah; the fragmentation is what human beings did with it.

Ibn Kathir identifies the fracture line concretely: *the nations were divided over their Messengers; some of them believed in them and some rejected them.* The primary split, in other words, was over the messengers themselves. Every prophet in this sūrah arrived with the same message and met the same division: some who believed, some who rejected.

**كُلٌّ إِلَيۡنَا رَٰجِعُونَ** — "They all shall return to Us." Ibn Kathir explains: *on the Day of Resurrection, when We will requite each person according to his deeds. If they are good, then he will be rewarded and if they are evil then he will be punished.*

This is the Qur'an's answer to the scandal of division. The splintering is real, and it is not going to be resolved by argument in this world. But it is temporary. Every faction and every individual who walked off with a scrap of the cloth is walking a road that ends in the same place — before Allah. *Kullun* — "all of them," with no exception clause. The disagreement will be settled by the One who gave the religion in the first place.

## Ayah 94: nothing you did for Allah is lost

After the sobering picture of ayah 93, ayah 94 arrives like a hand on the shoulder of the believer.

**فَمَن يَعۡمَلۡ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنٞ** — "So whoever does righteous good deeds while he is a believer."

Two conditions, and Ibn Kathir states them as a pair: *his heart believes and his deeds are righteous.* Inward and outward. The clause **وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنٞ** — "while he is a believer" — describes a state, not an extra task: the deed is done *from within* faith. This is the standing of one who did not join the tearing-apart of ayah 93 but held to the one path of ayah 92.

**فَلَا كُفۡرَانَ لِسَعۡيِهِۦ** — literally, "there shall be no *kufrān* for his *saʿy*," rendered in the translation as: he *"will never be denied"*; Ibn Kathir renders it *"his efforts will not be rejected."*

Two things are worth pausing on. First, the word for what is being protected is *saʿy* — striving, effort, exertion. Not "result," not "achievement." What is guaranteed is the treatment of your *effort*, which is the only part of it you ever controlled.

Second, the negation is total: *lā kufrāna* — there will be **no** denial of it whatsoever. Ibn Kathir explains this by the ayah *"certainly We shall not make the reward of anyone who does his deeds in the most perfect manner to be lost"* (18:30), and then draws out the meaning: *his efforts will not be wasted; they will be appreciated and not even a speck of dust's weight of injustice will be done.*

Read that carefully — it is not only that nothing is lost. It is that the effort is *appreciated*.

**وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ كَٰتِبُونَ** — "Verily, We record it for him." Ibn Kathir: *all his deeds are recorded and nothing of them at all is lost.* The word is *kātibūn* — "recorders," writers. The deed that no human being noticed, that produced no visible fruit, that you yourself have long forgotten, is written and kept. Note also the *lahu* — "**for** him." The record here is not a case being built against you; it is an asset being held in your name.

## Living it

**Hold the one path.** Ayah 92 marks the road and ayah 93 shows what people did to it. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's reading is the practical one: this ayah tells you what to avoid and what to do. Fragmenting the religion into sects is a human act, and it is the failure the passage sets before you.

**Get the creed right first.** The prophets' brotherhood is in worshipping Allah alone with no partner or associate — that, and not the details of law that varied between them, is the trunk the whole tree grows from.

**Keep the two conditions together.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 94 — the heart believes and the deeds are righteous — is a standing self-check. Faith that never moves the limbs, and action with nothing behind it, are both outside what ayah 94 guarantees.

**Stop measuring your deeds by their visible results.** The guarantee attaches to *saʿy*, your striving, and the recording is done by Allah Himself. The prophets in this sūrah were met with belief from some and rejection from others; their effort was not diminished by that in the slightest.

**Let ayah 93 comfort you about the divisions you cannot fix.** "They all shall return to Us." You are not required to settle the world's fractures. You are required to stay on the one path, do what is righteous, and trust the accounting to the One who is doing the recording.

passages.title: No return, until Gog and Magog
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close the door on a hope people quietly cling to: the hope of a second chance in this world. A nation destroyed for its rejection does not come back — and it will not come back right up until the world itself is ending, when Ya'juj and Ma'juj (Gog and Magog) are let loose and the true promise draws near. What binds the passage together is a single unbroken line drawn from the moment of destruction, across all of history, to the Day of Resurrection: no return, no return, no return — and then the horrified stare of those who spent their lives not thinking about this.

## Ayah 95 — the sentence that cannot be appealed

**"And a ban is laid on every town which We have destroyed that they shall not return."**

The word at the head of the ayah is *ḥarām*, rendered here as "a ban" — and in Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān's translation, "it is banned." Ibn 'Abbas explained it with one word: **"it is enforced."** That is, it has been decreed that the people of each township that has been destroyed will never return to this world before the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir notes that this is reported clearly from Ibn 'Abbas and likewise from Abu Ja'far al-Baqir, Qatadah and others.

Notice how the sentence is built. Allah does not simply say "they will not return." He says a ban *is laid upon the town* that they shall not return. What stands between them and any second chance is not their own weakness; it is something decreed, and, in Ibn 'Abbas's word, enforced. Ibn Kathir sums the ayah up in a single line: those who have been destroyed will never return to this world.

**Two readings among the commentators.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān reports (citing Qurtubi) that the commentators have given the ayah two different senses:

1. That the town and its people whom Allah destroyed cannot come back to life;
2. That it is binding upon the destroyed town that it shall not return to this world.

Both land in the same place, and Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws the conclusion out plainly: **the door of repentance is closed after death.** It is no longer possible for someone to return to this world and atone for his sins by performing righteous deeds. The final court will take place on the Day of Judgment.

## Ayah 96 — "until Ya'juj and Ma'juj are let loose"

**"Until, when Ya'juj and Ma'juj are let loose, and they swoop down from every ḥadab."**

At first glance the "until" seems to promise an exception: they will not return *until* Ya'juj and Ma'juj appear — as if then they might. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān heads that off directly. In the previous ayah it was said that those who died in a state of unbelief will never return to this world; the phrase "until Ya'juj and Ma'juj appear" really means that such people **will never return**, because the appearance of Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be a sign that the Day of Judgment is near at hand. The ban runs to the very edge of the world's life — and at that edge there is no world left to return to.

So the two ayat are one movement: the first closes the door, the second shows you the wall it is set in, stretching all the way to the end.

### "Let loose" — the force in *futiḥat*

The Arabic word used of them is *futiḥat*, which Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān renders "released" — meaning to let loose. And Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān draws the implication out: this **suggests that until the appointed time they remain under restraint, confined behind some barrier**, from which they will be released when the Day of Judgment is near. It adds that it is evident from the Qur'an that this restraint is the wall made by Dhul-Qarnayn, which will disappear near the Hour; and it refers the reader to Surah al-Kahf, where Ya'juj and Ma'juj and Dhul-Qarnayn are described in fair detail.

Ibn Kathir points to that very passage. Allah says, quoting Dhul-Qarnayn of his barrier: *"This is a mercy from my Lord, but when the promise of my Lord comes, He shall level it down to the ground. And the promise of my Lord is ever true. And on that Day, We shall leave them to surge like waves on one another"* (18:98–99).

Hold those two words together as the ayah places them: the barrier is **a mercy** — and it stands only until the promise of his Lord comes.

### "From every height, they come pouring"

*Wa hum min kulli ḥadabin yansilūn.* A ***ḥadab***, Ibn Kathir reports, is a raised portion of land — the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Abu Salih, ath-Thawri and others. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān says it means an elevated place, which may be a mountain or just a lump in the ground. And Ibn Kathir glosses the whole phrase this way: **they will come forth quickly to spread corruption.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān notes that the place where they are confined is somewhere beyond the northern mountains, so when they come out they will be seen rushing down the mountainsides in their hordes.

Ibn Kathir's remark on the phrasing is worth keeping: this is how their emergence is described, *as if the listener can see it*. You are not given a report; you are given a picture — every ridge and rise on the horizon suddenly moving, pouring downhill, from everywhere at once.

There is a small, unforgettable scene preserved here. Ibn Jarir narrated that 'Ubaydullah bin Abi Yazid said: **Ibn 'Abbas saw some young boys playing and pouncing on one another, and said, "This is how Ya'juj and Ma'juj will emerge."** A tumbling, swarming, unstoppable rush — he found the image in a courtyard of children.

### Who they are

Ibn Kathir states that they are from the progeny of Adam (peace be upon him), and also descendants of Nuh through his son Yafith (Japheth), who was the father of the Turks — "Turk" here referring to that group of them who were left behind the barrier built by Dhul-Qarnayn.

**And how do we know any of this?** Ibn Kathir answers by quoting Allah's own words: *"And none can inform you like Him Who is the All-Knower"* (35:14). This is information given by the One Who knows what has happened and what is yet to come, the One Who knows the unseen in the heavens and on earth. There is no god except Him. That is the only ground on which anyone can speak about the future at all — which is why speculation here is worthless and revelation is everything.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir notes that their emergence has been described in numerous hadiths of the Prophet ﷺ, and gathers several.

**Imam Ahmad recorded** that Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said he heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say that Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be let loose and will emerge upon mankind — *"and they swoop down from every ḥadab"* — overwhelming the people, so that the Muslims retreat to their cities and strongholds, bringing their flocks with them. They will drink all the water of the land, until some of them pass a river and drink it dry, and those coming after them pass that place and say, *"There used to be water here once."* When no one is left except those in their strongholds and cities, one of them will say: "We have defeated the people of the earth; now the people of heaven are left." One of them will shake his spear and hurl it into the sky, and it will come back stained with blood — as a test and a trial for them. While this is happening, Allah will send a worm in their necks, like the worm found in date-stones or in the nostrils of sheep, and they will die and their clamour will cease. Then the Muslims will ask who will volunteer to find out what the enemy is doing; one will step forward, knowing he will likely be killed, and will go down and find them dead, lying on top of one another, and will call out: *"O Muslims! Rejoice that Allah has sufficed you against your enemy!"* Then they will come out of their cities and strongholds and let their flocks graze — and they will have nothing to graze upon but the flesh of those people, and it will fill them better than any vegetation they have ever eaten. Ibn Kathir adds that **it was also recorded by Ibn Majah**.

Read that ending carefully. The mightiest force ever released upon the earth — one that drinks rivers dry and imagines itself at war with heaven — is finished not by an army but by a worm that Allah sends. The believers' part in it is patience behind their walls, and then one man's courage to go and look.

**Imam Ahmad also recorded** from an-Nawwas bin Sam'an al-Kilabi the long hadith in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned the Dajjal one morning, saying: *"There are other things that I fear for you more than the Dajjal. If he emerges while I am among you, I will deal with him for you. If he emerges when I am not among you, then each man will have to deal with him for himself, and Allah will take care of each Muslim on my behalf… O servants of Allah, be steadfast!"* He described his forty days — one day like a year, one like a month, one like a week, and the rest like your days — and when the Companions asked whether one day's and night's prayers would suffice for the day that is like a year, he said: **"No, but you will have to compute it according to its due proportion (and pray accordingly)."** A striking answer: even in that trial, the prayers are not folded up; the believer works out their proper measure and keeps praying.

He went on to describe how the Dajjal will call a people and they will respond, and he will command the sky and it will rain and the earth and it will bring forth vegetation; and how he will call another people who refuse, and drought will follow them. Then Allah will send the Messiah 'Isa son of Maryam, who will come down at the white minaret on the eastern side of Damascus, wearing two garments lightly dyed with saffron, his hands resting on the wings of two angels, and will catch up with the Dajjal at the eastern gate of Ludd and kill him. Then Allah will reveal to 'Isa: *"I have brought forth from amongst My creatures people against whom none will be able to fight. Take My servants safely to the Mount."* Then Allah will send Ya'juj and Ma'juj — and here the ayah is recited: *"and they swoop down from every ḥadab."*

'Isa and his companions will beseech Allah, and He will send insects against their necks, and in the morning they will all perish as one. They will come down and find no spot on earth free of the stench, and will beseech Allah again, and He will send birds with necks like those of Bactrian camels, which will carry them and throw them wherever Allah wills. Then Allah will send rain for forty days that no house of clay nor tent of camel's hair can keep out, until the earth is washed and left looking like a mirror; and it will be said to the earth: bring forth your fruit and restore your blessing. On that day a group of people will eat from one pomegranate and take shade under its skin, and one milch-camel will suffice a whole group of people. Then Allah will send a pleasant wind which will take the soul of every Muslim — or every believer — and there will be left only the most evil of people, and upon them the Hour will come. Ibn Kathir notes this **was also recorded by Muslim but not by al-Bukhari**, and by the Sunan compilers with different chains of narrators, and that **at-Tirmidhi said: "It is Hasan Sahih."**

**Imam Ahmad recorded** from Ibn Harmalah, from his maternal aunt, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave a khutbah with a bandage on his finger where he had been stung by a scorpion, and said: *"You say that you have no enemy, but you will keep fighting your enemies until Ya'juj and Ma'juj come, with their wide faces, small eyes and reddish hair, pouring down from every mound with their faces looking like burnished shields."* Ibn Abi Hatim recorded something similar through another chain.

Ibn Kathir adds that it was confirmed by hadiths that 'Isa son of Maryam will perform Hajj to the Ancient House, the Ka'bah. **Imam Ahmad recorded** that Abu Sa'id said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"He will certainly come to this House and perform Hajj and 'Umrah, after the emergence of Ya'juj and Ma'juj."* Ibn Kathir notes this **was recorded by al-Bukhari**.

And Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān cites the **Sahih of Muslim**, from Sayyiduna Hudhaifah (may Allah be pleased with him): he and some other Companions were in the midst of a discussion when the Prophet ﷺ came and asked what they were deliberating; they said they were discussing the Day of Judgment, and he said that it will occur only after ten signs have become manifest — and the appearance of Ya'juj and Ma'juj will be one of them.

## Ayah 97 — the promise draws near, and the eyes freeze

**"And the true promise shall draw near. Then, you shall see the eyes of the disbelievers fixedly staring in horror."**

*Al-wa'd al-ḥaqq*, "the true promise," is the Day of Resurrection — the Day, says Ibn Kathir, when these terrors and earthquakes and this chaos will come to pass. The Hour has drawn nigh, and when it comes to pass the disbelievers will say: "This is a difficult Day." It is the same promise named in the ayah of al-Kahf quoted above, where the barrier stands until *"the promise of my Lord"* comes — *"and the promise of my Lord is ever true."*

Then the ayah gives us the disbelievers themselves — *fa idhā hiya shākhiṣatun abṣāru alladhīna kafarū*, their eyes **fixedly staring in horror**. Ibn Kathir's explanation is simply: because of the horror of the tremendous events that they are witnessing. There is no argument left in the scene, no debate — first their eyes, then their words.

**"Woe to us! We were indeed heedless of this — nay, but we were wrongdoers."**

Two confessions, and the second corrects the first. *"We were indeed heedless of this"* means, Ibn Kathir explains, heedless **in the world** — it simply was not on their minds. But then: *"nay, but we were wrongdoers."* Heedlessness sounds almost like an excuse — we weren't paying attention, we weren't thinking about it. They abandon that excuse themselves and name it as wrongdoing. And Ibn Kathir's comment on it is quietly devastating: **they will admit their wrongdoing at the time when that will not help them at all.**

## Living it

Put the three ayat back together and the practical weight of the passage is plain.

**The one confession that counts is the one made now.** The disbelievers in ayah 97 say exactly the right thing — "we were wrongdoers" — and Ibn Kathir tells us plainly that it will not help them at all, because ayah 95 has already closed the door behind them: the door of repentance, as Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān puts it, is closed after death. The very same words said today, in a moment of privacy, are a different thing entirely. The difference is not in the words. It is in the timing.

**Heedlessness is not innocence.** They begin by pleading that they were heedless "in the world" and end by naming it wrongdoing. A life spent not thinking about this Day is not a neutral life.

**Fear the barrier, not the horde.** Ya'juj and Ma'juj are held behind a wall that Allah's ayah calls a mercy, and when they finally come they are destroyed at His command by a worm He sends. What the passage asks of the believer is not calculation but readiness — to be among those who were not heedless when the true promise drew near — and, as the Prophet ﷺ said in the hadith of an-Nawwas recorded by Imam Ahmad: *"O servants of Allah, be steadfast!"*

passages.title: Idols as fuel, the righteous kept safe
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat set two destinies side by side: idols as fuel, and the righteous kept safe. The false gods and the people who worshipped them end up in the same fire, the idols themselves serving as its fuel. Then, without pause, the passage turns and shows the opposite destiny — believers carried so far from that fire that not even a whisper of it reaches them, greeted by angels on the Day they were always promised. What holds ayat 98–103 together is that contrast, and a real historical argument in Makkah that these very words provoked.

## The scene in the masjid

Ibn Kathīr preserves an account from Muhammad bin Ishāq bin Yasār, in his book of Sīrah, that unlocks this whole passage.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting one day in the Masjid with Al-Walīd bin Al-Mughīrah. An-Nadr bin Al-Hārith came and sat with them, and other men of Quraysh were present. The Prophet ﷺ spoke; An-Nadr came at him in argument, and the Prophet ﷺ answered him until he defeated him. Then he recited to An-Nadr and to the whole gathering:

> "Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are but fuel for Hell! Surely you will enter it" — through to — "and therein they will hear not." (21:98–100)

Then the Prophet ﷺ got up and went to sit with 'Abdullāh bin Az-Zab'arī As-Sahmī. Al-Walīd said to Ibn Az-Zab'arī: "By Allah, An-Nadr bin Al-Hārith could not match the son of 'Abd Al-Muttalib in argument. Muhammad claims that we and these gods that we worship are fuel for Hell."

Ibn Az-Zab'arī answered: "By Allah, if I meet with him I will defeat him in argument." His objection was this — ask Muhammad whether *everyone* who is worshipped besides Allah goes into Hell along with those who worshipped him. Because, he said, we worship the angels, the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Christians worship Al-Masīh, 'Īsā bin Maryam. Al-Walīd and those sitting with him were amazed and thought he had come up with a good point.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same episode from a different angle, quoting Qurtubī's report from Ibn 'Abbās. Ibn 'Abbās used to wonder aloud that there was an ayah in the Qur'an people had reservations about, yet nobody came to ask him about it — either they had already found a convincing answer, he said, or they were simply indifferent and did not think the matter important enough to investigate. When they asked which ayah, he recited *innakum wa mā ta'budūn* and explained: when it came down, the disbelievers of Quraysh were furious, feeling it offended their gods, so they went to Ibn al-Zibaʻrā — described there as a scholar of the scriptures — to complain. He told them that had he been present he would have given a reply that would have confounded all of them; pressed further, he produced the argument about the Messiah and 'Uzayr. Quraysh were delighted and certain the Prophet ﷺ would have no answer.

## The answer

The objection was put to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and Ibn Kathīr records his reply — again through Ibn Ishāq's Sīrah, so we relay the teaching without attaching it to any hadith collection:

> "Everyone who likes to be worshipped instead of Allah will be with the ones who worshipped him, for indeed they are worshipping the Shaytān and whoever told them to worship him."

That is the pivot. The criterion is not *who was worshipped* but *who wanted it*. A creature who liked being worshipped instead of Allah is with those who worshipped him — and what such worshippers are really serving, the words say, is Shaytān and whoever instructed them.

Then, Ibn Kathīr says, Allah revealed ayat 101–102: **"Verily, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, they will be removed far therefrom. They shall not hear the slightest sound of it, while they abide in that which their own selves desire."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way: those for whom Allah's grace and good result is ensured will be kept away from Hell.

Some of the early scholars therefore read ayah 101 as a deliberate exception made after ayah 98 — an exception in the case of those who are worshipped instead of Allah, excluding 'Uzayr and the Messiah from their number. Ibn Kathīr transmits this from Hajjāj bin Muhammad Al-A'war from Ibn Jurayj, and from 'Uthmān bin 'Atā' from Ibn 'Abbās; and it was said that the exception referred to the angels, 'Īsā, and others who are worshipped instead of Allah — the view of 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Kathīr adds that it was revealed about the mention of 'Īsā, 'Uzayr, and the rabbis and monks who were also worshipped — people who had spent their lives in devotion towards Allah, until the misguided people who came after them took them as lords instead of Allah.

Connected to the same dispute, Ibn Kathīr notes, came the passage on the notion of worshipping the angels as daughters of Allah — *"And they say: 'The Most Gracious has begotten children.' Glory to Him! They are but honoured slaves"* … *"And if any of them should say: 'Verily, I am a god besides Him,' such a one We should recompense with Hell"* (21:26–29) — and, concerning 'Īsā bin Maryam and the amazement of Al-Walīd and those present at Ibn Az-Zab'arī's argument, the passage in Sūrah az-Zukhruf: *"And when the son of Maryam is quoted as an example, behold, your people cry aloud. And say: 'Are our gods better or is he?' They quoted not the above example except for argument. Nay! But they are a quarrelsome people. He was not more than a slave. We granted Our favour to him"* (43:57–61). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise reports that when Ibn al-Zibaʻrā put forward the example of Maryam (peace be upon her), the people of his clan, Quraysh, were overtaken by joy — and that 43:57 was revealed for that same Ibn al-Zibaʻrā.

## Why the objection was a mistake

Ibn Kathīr is direct: what Ibn Az-Zab'arī said was a serious mistake. The ayah was addressed to the people of Makkah concerning *their* worship of idols — idols which, as Ibn Kathīr puts it, were inanimate and could not think. It was a rebuke for their worship of them. And so Ibn Kathīr asks: how could this be applied to Al-Masīh, 'Uzayr and others who did righteous deeds and did not accept the worship of those who worshipped them?

This is worth pausing on for anyone who meets the same objection today. Ibn Az-Zab'arī won applause by taking words addressed to Makkan idolaters about their lifeless idols and stretching them to cover prophets and angels. Ibn Kathīr's reply, and the Prophet's ﷺ before it, is that these words must be read in the situation they address.

## Fuel: the word *hasab*

The word the Qur'an chooses in ayah 98 is **حَصَب (hasab)**, and the early authorities gathered by Ibn Kathīr circle it from several sides:

- **Ibn 'Abbās:** "Kindling" — and Ibn Kathīr links it to *"whose fuel is men and stones"* (66:6).
- **Ibn 'Abbās**, in another report: it means *firewood* in the dialect of the people of Zanjiyyah.
- **Mujāhid, 'Ikrimah and Qatādah:** "Its fuel."
- **Ad-Dahhāk:** "The fuel of Hell means that which is thrown into it" — and Ibn Kathīr notes this was also the view of others.

Feel the humiliation packed into that. Ad-Dahhāk's gloss in particular strips the idols of every trace of the dignity their worshippers gave them: they are named as *what gets thrown in* — the Fire's material, not its masters. And notice how ayah 98 sorts them: the worshippers and the objects of their worship land in a single category, fuel, exactly as the parallel Ibn Kathīr cites does — "men and stones."

**"Surely you will enter it"** — *antum lahā wāridūn*. Ibn Kathīr's gloss is plain and heavy: "you will go into it."

Ayah 99 then delivers the logical stroke: **"Had these been gods, they would not have entered there."** Ibn Kathīr spells it out — if these idols and false gods you worshipped instead of Allah had really been gods, they would not have entered the Hellfire. A god who cannot keep himself out of the Fire was never a god. **"And all of them will abide therein forever"** — Ibn Kathīr: the worshippers and the objects of their worship will all abide therein forever.

## The sound of the Fire, and the silence

Ayah 100 gives the Fire a soundtrack: **"Therein they will be breathing out with deep sighs and roaring."** Ibn Kathīr connects it to *"they will have in the Fire, zafīr and shahīq"* (11:106), and defines the pair precisely — **زَفِير (zafīr)** refers to their exhalation, **شَهِيق (shahīq)** to their inhalation. Not speech, not argument, not appeal: raw breathing, in and out. The confident arguers of ayah 98 are reduced to lungs.

And then: **"and therein they will hear not."** The one thing they will produce is noise; the one thing they will not receive is anything worth hearing.

## Those for whom the good has already gone ahead

Ayah 101 turns the page. **"Verily, those for whom the good (al-husnā) has preceded from Us."** On what *al-husnā* means, Ibn Kathīr reports: **'Ikrimah said, "Mercy."** Others said it means being blessed.

Notice the verb: *sabaqat* — it has **preceded**, gone ahead of them. The blessing was already in place before their lives ran their course. This is not a reward invented at the last moment; it is Allah's prior grace meeting the deeds it produced.

Ibn Kathīr explains the structure of the passage exactly as a reader feels it: when Allah mentions the people of Hell and their punishment for associating others in worship with Him, He follows it with a description of the blessed who believed in Allah and His Messengers. These are the ones for whom the blessing has preceded from Allah, and who did righteous deeds in the world — as Allah says, *"For those who have done good is the best reward and even more"* (10:26), and *"Is there any reward for good other than good?"* (55:60). Ibn Kathīr's summary: just as they did good in this world, Allah will make their final destiny and their reward good; He will save them from punishment and give them a great reward.

**"They will be removed far therefrom"** — *mub'adūn*, moved to a distance. Ayah 102 measures that distance by sound: **"They shall not hear the slightest sound of it."** The word is **حَسِيس (hasīs)** — the faintest audible trace. Ibn Kathīr's comment goes further than hearing: it means **they will not feel its heat in their bodies.** Not a rustle, not a warmth.

Set that beside ayah 100 and the symmetry is exact. The people of the Fire hear nothing; the people of Paradise hear nothing *of the Fire*. One deafness is deprivation, the other is protection.

**"While they abide in that which their own selves desire."** Ibn Kathīr: they will be safe from that which they fear, and they will have all that they love and desire. Both halves of the human heart are answered at once — the fear emptied out, the longing filled — and *khālidūn*, permanently.

## "The greatest terror will not grieve them"

Ayah 103 opens with **الفَزَعُ الأكبر (al-fazaʻ al-akbar)**, the greatest terror. The commentators genuinely differ on what it refers to, and the sources name the views rather than settling them:

- **That it means death** — as was narrated by 'Abdur-Razzāq from Yahyā bin Rabī'ah from 'Atā'.
- **That it refers to the blast of the Trumpet** — as Al-'Awfī said narrating from Ibn 'Abbās, and Abū Sinān, Sa'īd bin Sinān Ash-Shaybānī. **This was the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr in his Tafsīr.**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refines the second position. It reports **Ibn 'Abbās** as saying the greatest terror refers to the **second** call of the Horn, when all the dead will assemble to give an account of their actions in the world; **some others** said it is the **first** call of the Horn. **Ibn Al-'Arabī** held that the Horn will be blown three times: the first, *nafkhat al-fazaʻ*, which will put everyone into utter confusion — this being *al-fazaʻ al-akbar*; the second, *nafkhat al-saʻq*, when everyone will die; the third, *nafkhat al-baʻth*, when all the dead will be resurrected. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds (citing Mazharī) that this version derives support from a hadith of Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, quoted in **Musnad Abū Yaʻlā** and **Baihaqī, 'Abd Ibn Humaid, Abū al-Sheikh, Ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī** and others.

Whichever it is, the promise is the same, and note its precision: the ayah does not say the terror will not occur. It says it **will not grieve them**. The Day will still be what it is; their hearts will simply not be broken by it.

## The welcome

**"And the angels will meet them, with the greeting: 'This is your Day which you were promised.'"** Ibn Kathīr explains that the angels will greet them on the Day of Resurrection when they emerge from their graves with these words — and his gloss on the greeting is beautifully simple: *hope for the best*.

Think of the reversal. Ayah 98 begins with a crowd of confident men in a Makkan masjid, sure their gods will stand by them. Ayah 103 ends with a different crowd rising from the earth into a reception party of angels, told that the Day they were warned about all along is in fact *their* Day.

## Living it

**Judge what you serve by whether it can save itself.** That is the whole argument of ayah 99, as Ibn Kathīr reads it: had they really been gods, they would not have entered the Hellfire. Anything you organise your life around — stone, status, appetite, an opinion of you — apply the test: can it keep itself out of the Fire? If not, it cannot keep you out either.

**Beware the applause of a clever argument.** Quraysh were "amazed" at Ibn al-Zibaʻrā's point and thought he had come up with a good point; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says they were delighted, overtaken by joy. Their pleasure was in scoring, not in truth. Of exactly such disputing the Qur'an says they quoted the example only for argument — *"Nay! But they are a quarrelsome people"* (43:57–61). A debate won against revelation is a debate lost.

**Do not let devotion drift into veneration.** Ibn Kathīr's note that righteous ones — 'Īsā, 'Uzayr, rabbis and monks — had spent their lives in devotion towards Allah before later, misguided generations took them as lords instead of Allah is a warning aimed at the admirers of the pious, not at the pious themselves. Love the righteous; direct worship to Allah alone.

**Live now toward *al-husnā*.** The blessing has "preceded" from Allah for those who then did righteous deeds in the world (10:26; 55:60). The believer's part of that equation is today's deeds. And the reward is defined not just as pleasure but as **safety** — safe from what is feared, given all that is loved.

passages.title: The heavens rolled up like a scroll
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat take us to the far end of time and then, in the same breath, tell us that the ending was written down long before it arrived. Ayah 104 shows the sky itself being folded away like a scroll and the whole creation begun again; ayah 105 tells us that the outcome of that Day — who ends up inheriting the land — was already recorded. What holds the two together is a single idea: **what is coming is not a possibility, it is a promise already entered in writing.**

## The sky folded like a page

*"On that Day We will roll up the heavens like a scroll of writings"* (ayah 104).

Ibn Kathir explains that this describes what will happen on the Day of Resurrection, and he places it beside another ayah that shows the same scene from a different angle:

> "They made not a just estimate of Allah such as is due to Him. And on the Day of Resurrection the whole of the earth will be grasped by His Hand and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand. Glorified be He, and High be He above all that they associate as partners with Him!" (39:67)

Notice what the image does to your sense of scale. The Qur'an compares the folding of the heavens to the small, ordinary motion of rolling up a written page. Nothing is strained; nothing is difficult. It is the gesture of a hand closing a document that has been fully written. And notice how the ayah closes: the mention of the Right Hand is followed immediately by *"Glorified be He, and High be He above all that they associate as partners with Him."* The glorification is part of the same sentence — we say it as Allah said it, and we let His own words about His transcendence stand alongside it.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites that al-Bukhari recorded, from Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will seize the earth and the heavens will be in His Right Hand."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays a report from Ibn 'Umar as it appears in Sahih al-Bukhari: that on the Day of Judgement Allah would roll up all the seven skies and the seven worlds along with all the created things upon them in His hand, and all of them together would be no more than a grain of rye in His hand.

## What a *sijill* is

The Arabic reads *ka-ṭayyi's-sijilli lil-kutub* — "like the rolling up of the *sijill* for the *kutub*." Two words need opening up.

Ibn Kathir says that what is meant by *Sijill* is a book. He then reports that **as-Suddi** understood *as-Sijill* to be an angel entrusted with the records: when a person dies his book of deeds is taken up to As-Sijill, who rolls it up and puts it away until the Day of Resurrection. But Ibn Kathir says the correct view is the one narrated from **Ibn 'Abbas** — that *as-Sijill* refers to the record of deeds itself. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas by 'Ali bin Abi Talhah and al-'Awfi; it was also stated by **Mujahid**, **Qatadah** and others, and it was the view favoured by **Ibn Jarir**, because this usage is well known in the Arabic language. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists the same line of authorities for taking *sijill* to mean a sheet of a book: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ali Ibn Abi Talhah, 'Awfi, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Kathir.

The second word, *al-kutub*, literally "the books," is used here — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes — in the sense of *al-maktūb*, "that which is written." So the meaning of the verse is that the sky will be rolled up like a scroll with its writings: a scroll closing over everything inscribed in it.

**A linguistic parallel.** Having settled the meaning, Ibn Kathir says the sense is simply *the Day when the heaven will be rolled up like a scroll*, and he supports the reading with another ayah:

> "Then, when they had both submitted themselves (to the will of Allah), and he had laid him prostrate on his forehead." (37:103)

He adds that there are many more linguistic examples in this respect, and closes with the scholar's habit of humility: *Allah knows best.*

There is a quiet resonance worth feeling here. On the reading Ibn Kathir prefers, the *sijill* is a record of deeds — and the sky is folded the way such a record is folded. In the very next ayah we are told about something Allah *wrote*. Creation, from this angle, reads like a document: opened, filled, and closed at its appointed time.

## "As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it"

The second half of ayah 104 turns from the folding of the sky to the raising of the dead.

Ibn Kathir's answer is compact and complete: this will inevitably come to pass on the Day when Allah creates His creation anew — **as He created them in the first place, He is surely able to re-create them.** The One who produced something the first time is not going to be defeated by producing it a second time.

Then comes the seal: *wa'dan 'alaynā* — "a promise binding upon Us." Ibn Kathir explains that this must inevitably come to pass because it is one of the things Allah has promised, and **He does not break His promise**, and He is able to do it — which is why the ayah ends *innā kunnā fā'ilīn*, "Truly, We shall do it." Power without a promise might leave room for doubt about whether it will be exercised; a promise without power would be empty. Here both are stated together, and the matter is closed.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood among them exhorting them and said:

> "You will be gathered before Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. *As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it. (It is) a promise binding upon Us. Truly, We shall do it.*"

Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded in the Two Sahihs, and that al-Bukhari mentioned it in his Tafsir of this very ayah. Look at what the Prophet ﷺ did with the verse: he took "as We began the first creation" and made it concrete. You will return exactly as you first arrived — with nothing on you, nothing added to you, nothing carried in your hands. Every layer a person spends a lifetime acquiring is left behind at the threshold. That is what "repeating the first creation" feels like from the inside.

## Ayah 105: the verdict was written before the Day arrived

*"And indeed We have written in az-Zabūr after adh-Dhikr that My righteous servants shall inherit the land."*

Having shown the folding of the sky, the passage now shows the ledger. Ibn Kathir frames the ayah as Allah telling us of **His decree for His righteous servants** — those who are the blessed in this world and in the Hereafter, and who will inherit the earth in this world and in the Hereafter. And he stresses the point of the wording: Allah tells us that this **is recorded** in the Books of Divine Laws and Decrees, and that it will inevitably come to pass. The believer's future is not a hope pinned on events; it is an entry in a book.

Ibn Kathir brings three ayat as parallels for that decree:

- *"Verily, the earth is Allah's. He gives it as a heritage to whom He wills of His servants; and the (blessed) end is for those who have Taqwa."* (7:128)
- *"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth."* (40:51)
- *"Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous good deeds, that He will certainly grant them succession in the land, as He granted it to those before them, and that He will grant them the authority to practise their religion which He has chosen for them."* (24:55)

### What are "az-Zabūr" and "adh-Dhikr"?

Here the commentators genuinely differ, and both sources lay the views out rather than settling them:

- **Sa'īd bin Jubayr** — asked by al-A'mash about this ayah — said: "*Az-Zabūr* means the Tawrah, the Injīl and the Qur'an."
- **Ibn 'Abbas, ash-Sha'bī, al-Hasan, Qatādah** and others said: *az-Zabūr* is that which was revealed to Dāwūd (peace be upon him), and *adh-Dhikr* is the Tawrah.
- **Mujāhid** said *az-Zabūr* means the Book; and in another statement, that it means the Books which came after *adh-Dhikr*, *adh-Dhikr* being **Umm al-Kitāb**, the Mother of the Book, which is with Allah.
- **Zayd bin Aslam** said it is the First Book; **ath-Thawrī** said it is **al-Lawh al-Mahfūz**, the Preserved Tablet.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the linguistic root of the disagreement: *zabūr* is the plural of *zubur*, meaning "book," and it is also the name of the book revealed to Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him) — and opinions differ as to which sense is intended here. It reports, via Ibn Jarīr, a version attributed to Ibn 'Abbas in which *adh-Dhikr* refers to the Torah and *az-Zabūr* to all the books revealed after the Torah — the Zabūr, the Injīl and the Qur'an — the same explanation adopted by **Dahhāk**. It also reports from **Ibn Zayd**, an explanation **Zajjāj** likewise adopted, that *adh-Dhikr* refers to al-Lawh al-Mahfūz and *az-Zabūr* to all the books revealed to the prophets.

The views converge on one thing even while they differ on the labels: **this promise is old.** Whether the earlier record is the Torah or the Preserved Tablet, the inheritance of the righteous was written before it was announced here — which is precisely why the ayah opens with the emphatic *wa laqad katabnā*, "and We certainly did write."

### Which "land" do they inherit?

Ibn Kathir reports that **Mujāhid, narrating from Ibn 'Abbas**, said this means **the land of Paradise** — and that this was also the view of Abū 'Āliyah, Mujāhid, Sa'īd bin Jubayr, ash-Sha'bī, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Abū Sālih, ar-Rabī' bin Anas and ath-Thawrī (may Allah have mercy on them).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says all commentators agree the word here refers to the land of Paradise, reporting this explanation from Ibn 'Abbas via Ibn Jarīr and noting that Mujāhid, Ibn Jubair, Ikrimah, Suddī and Abū al-'Āliyah adopted the same. It then gives the reasoning, which is worth following:

1. **Imam Rāzī** says another ayah of the Qur'an supports this reading, one where the same wording is used of Paradise: *"And has bequeathed upon us the earth for us to make our dwelling wheresoever we will in Paradise"* (39:74).
2. The verb is *inherit*. The land of this earth can be inherited by all, believers and non-believers alike — so a land specified for **the righteous** lends credence to reading it as the land of Paradise.
3. **Context.** The phrase follows the mention of the Qiyāmah, and it is well known that after the Qiyāmah there will be no land of this earth left, only the land of Paradise.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then records another version from Ibn 'Abbas: that "the land" means land as such, including both the land of this earth and the land of Paradise. On that reading the Paradise portion is obvious, and as for this world, the Qur'an states in several places that a time will come when the entire land of the world belongs to the pious believers — and here it cites the same ayat Ibn Kathir cited: 7:128, 24:55 and 40:51. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that history has already witnessed the control of the pious believers over the better part of the world, and that it will again come under their control during the time of Sayyidnā Mahdī (may Allah be pleased with him).

Note the honest shape of the difference: one group reads the inheritance as belonging to Paradise, the other reads it as covering both — and neither denies Paradise. The disagreement is about how much of this world is included in a promise everyone agrees culminates there.

## Living it

**Read your own life as a record.** On the reading Ibn Kathir prefers, *as-Sijill* is the record of deeds — a scroll rolled up over its own writing. Yours is being written now and will be rolled up in its turn. Whatever you would not want sealed into that page, do not write today.

**Let the first creation settle the second.** When the Hereafter feels abstract, Ibn Kathir's argument is the one to return to: as Allah created you in the first place, He is surely able to re-create you. You are already the proof.

**Arrive as you will be gathered.** The Prophet ﷺ said you will be gathered before Allah barefoot, naked and uncircumcised. Nothing you accumulate crosses that line. Hold the world with the grip of someone who knows what will be left at the door.

**Stake your claim in the right land.** Ayah 105 names the heirs: *'ibādiya as-sālihūn*, "My righteous servants." The inheritance is not attached to a lineage, a nation or an era — it is attached to a description, and a description is something a person can enter. As Ibn Kathir puts it, this is recorded in the Books of Divine Laws and Decrees and will inevitably come to pass. The title deed to the lasting land was written before you were born, and it names the servants who are righteous. Become one of them, and it names you.

passages.title: The Prophet's final proclamation and prayer

These seven ayat bring Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ to its close. After a long procession of prophets and their rejected calls, the sūrah turns to the last Messenger ﷺ and tells him what this whole recitation amounts to, what he himself is, what he must announce, what he does not know, and finally what he should pray. They hold together as one movement: **a sufficient message (106), a merciful messenger (107), a single demand (108), a clean parting if it is refused (109), the Knower of all speech and secrets (110), a delay that may itself be a test (111), and a prayer that hands the whole matter back to Allah (112).**

## "In this there is a plain Message" (106)

Ayah 106 points backwards — *"Verily, in **this** there is a plain Message."* Ibn Kathir explains it as: *in this Qur'an which We have revealed to Our servant Muhammad ﷺ, there is a plain Message which is beneficial and is sufficient for a people who worship Allah.*

Immediately before it, ayah 105 had promised that *"the land will be inherited by My righteous slaves,"* written already *"in az-Zabūr after adh-Dhikr."* The early scholars read those two names differently, and the sources preserve the disagreement rather than settling it:

- Al-Aʿmash said he asked Saʿīd bin Jubayr, who answered that **az-Zabūr means the Tawrāh, the Injīl and the Qur'an**.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās, ash-Shaʿbī, al-Hasan, Qatādah and others** said az-Zabūr is that which was revealed to Dāwūd, and adh-Dhikr is the Tawrāh.
- **Mujāhid** said in one report simply "the Book," and in another that az-Zabūr means the Books which came after adh-Dhikr, adh-Dhikr being *Umm al-Kitāb* — the Mother of the Book, which is with Allah. **Zayd bin Aslam** called it "the First Book," and **ath-Thawrī** identified it as al-Lawh al-Mahfūz, the Preserved Tablet.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *zabūr* is the plural of *zubur*, meaning "book," besides being the name of the book revealed to Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him); it notes that opinions differ on the meaning here, reports a version attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās in which *adh-Dhikr* is the Tawrāh and *az-Zabūr* all the books revealed after it — Zabūr, Injīl and Qur'an (from Ibn Jarīr, and the same explanation adopted by Dahhāk) — while Ibn Zayd, followed by Zajjāj, held that adh-Dhikr is the Preserved Tablet and az-Zabūr all the books revealed to the prophets.

As for **"the land"** that the righteous inherit: Mujāhid, narrating from Ibn ʿAbbās, said this means *the land of Paradise* — the view also of Abū ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ash-Shaʿbī, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Abū Sālih, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and ath-Thawrī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās through Ibn Jarīr, adopted also by Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Suddī and Abū al-ʿĀliyah, and notes Imām Rāzī's supporting argument from another ayah, *"And has bequeathed upon us the earth for us to make our dwelling wheresoever we will in Paradise"* (39:74) — with the further point that earthly land can be inherited by believer and disbeliever alike, whereas this promise is specific, and that the promise follows a mention of Qiyāmah, after which no earthly land remains, only the land of Paradise.

Another version from Ibn ʿAbbās takes "the land" to mean land as such, including both this world's land and Paradise's, since the Qur'an states in several places that the whole earth will one day belong to the pious believers: *"Surely, the land belongs to Allah. He lets whomsoever He wills, from among His slaves, inherit it. And the end-result is in favour of those who fear Allah"* (7:128); *"Allah has promised those of you who believe and do good deeds that He will certainly make them (His) vicegerents in the land"* (24:55); *"Surely, We shall help Our Messengers and those who have believed in the present life, and upon the day when the witnesses arise"* (40:51). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that history has already witnessed the control of the pious believers over the better part of the world, and that it will come under their control again in the time of Sayyidnā Mahdī. Ibn Kathir states plainly that this is recorded in the Books of Divine Laws and Decrees, and **it will inevitably come to pass**.

**Who is the message sufficient for?** The ayah does not say "for people who read" or "for people who argue" but *li-qawmin ʿābidīn* — **for a people who worship Allah**. Ibn Kathir defines them precisely: those who worship Allah *in the manner which He has prescribed and which He loves and is pleased with*, and who *would rather obey Allah than follow the Shaytān or their own desires*. That is a quiet but severe filter. On Ibn Kathir's reading the sufficiency lies in the message; the ayah names the ones it is sufficient *for* — those who prefer obedience to Allah over the Shaytān and their own appetite.

## "We sent you only as a mercy to the worlds" (107)

This is the most quoted ayah of the passage, and the sources unfold it in two directions — how wide the mercy is, and how it works.

**How wide.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *ʿālamīn* is the plural of *ʿālam*, "world," and includes **all creatures — humans, animals, plants, jinn**. The mercy is not scoped to the Arabs, or to Muslims, or even to mankind. Ibn Kathir: Allah *"sent him as a mercy for all of them."*

**How it works.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a striking explanation. The true essence of the entire universe is the invocation and worship of Allah; when that essence departs from this world and no one is left to worship Allah, everything in it will perish — that is the day Qiyāmah occurs. Once you grasp that the invocation and worship of Allah is the essence of all living things, the reason for calling him ﷺ "mercy to the worlds" becomes obvious: **it is his teachings and the purity of his personal life alone which keep the worship of Allah alive until Qiyāmah.**

That, Maʿārif continues, is why he declared, *"I am the blessing sent by Allah"* — cited from Ibn ʿAsākir, quoting Abū Hurayrah — and, in a report of Ibn ʿUmar which Maʿārif attributes to Ibn Kathir, *"I am the blessing sent by Allah, so that I lift up the people (who obey Allah) and humble the other people (who disobey Allah)."*

**Mercy in his temperament.** Muslim reports in his *Sahīh*, from Abū Hurayrah, that it was said, "O Messenger of Allah, pray against the idolaters," and he replied:

> *"I was not sent as a curse, rather I was sent as a mercy."*

Imām Ahmad recorded that ʿAmr bin Abī Qurrah al-Kindī said: Hudhayfah was in al-Madāʾin, mentioning things the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had said. Hudhayfah came to Salmān, and Salmān said: "O Hudhayfah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would sometimes be angry and would speak accordingly, and would sometimes be pleased and would speak accordingly. I know that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ addressed us and said:

> *"Any man of my Ummah whom I have insulted or cursed when I was angry — for I am a man from among the sons of Adam, and I get angry just as you do. But Allah has sent me as a Mercy to the Worlds, so I will make that (my anger) into blessings for him on the Day of Resurrection."*

Ibn Kathir adds that this was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd, from Ahmad bin Yūnus, from Zāʾidah. Note the honesty of it: a human being who feels anger, whose very anger is turned into blessings by the mercy for which Allah sent him.

**What mercy reaches those who reject him?** Ibn Kathir raises the question — *what kind of mercy do those who disbelieve in him get?* — and answers with a report of Ibn ʿAbbās recorded by Abū Jaʿfar bin Jarīr: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day has mercy decreed for him in this world and the Hereafter; whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger *"will be protected from that which happened to the nations of earthquakes and stoning."*

Ibn Kathir is careful, though, that mercy offered is not the same as mercy received: whoever accepts this mercy and gives thanks for this blessing *"will be happy in this world and in the Hereafter,"* but whoever rejects it and denies it *"will lose out in this world and in the Hereafter."* He cites *"Have you not seen those who have changed the blessings of Allah into disbelief, and caused their people to dwell in the house of destruction?"* (14:28-29), and *"Say: It is for those who believe, a guide and a healing. And as for those who disbelieve, there is heaviness in their ears, and it is blindness for them"* (41:44).

From this understanding of the ayah, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a conclusion: *it therefore follows that performing jihad against the unbelievers in order to lessen shirk and kufr (unbelief), and in the hope of reclaiming those who transgress the Divine Commands of Allah, is an act of mercy.*

## The proclamation: one demand, plainly put (108)

Ayah 108 compresses everything the sūrah has argued into a single sentence the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to say to the idolaters: *"It is revealed to me that your ilāh"* — the deity you serve — *"is only one ilāh."* Ibn Kathir's heading is worth keeping: **the main objective of revelation is that Allah be worshipped.** Not a philosophy, not a set of customs: that the One be worshipped.

Then the question — *fahal antum muslimūn*, "will you then be Muslims?" Ibn Kathir glosses it: *will you then follow that and submit to it?* Notice that the ayah does not command them to submit; it *asks*.

## If they turn away: notice on equal terms (109)

*"But if they turn away"* — Ibn Kathir: if they ignore that to which you call them — *"say: I give you a notice to be known to us all alike."* He explains it as: *'I declare that I am in a state of war with you as you are in a state of war with me. I have nothing to do with you just as you have nothing to do with me.'*

Ibn Kathir sets it beside *"If you fear treachery from any people, throw back (their covenant) to them (so as to be) on equal terms"* (8:58) — which means, he says, so that both you and they will know that the treaty is null and void. And beside *"For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do!"* (10:41). This is not a curse; it is a declared separation, announced so that both sides know exactly where they stand.

## Three things he does not know, and One who knows everything (109-111)

What follows is remarkable in a scripture: the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to state the limits of his own knowledge, twice.

**"And I know not whether that which you are promised is near or far"** (109). Ibn Kathir: *'it will inevitably come to pass, but I have no knowledge of whether it is near or far.'* His heading over these words is blunt — **no one knows when the Hour will come.** The Day of Resurrection is certain in its occurrence and hidden in its timing, and the one who receives revelation is told to say so openly.

**"Verily, He knows that which is spoken aloud and He knows that which you conceal"** (110). Set against his admitted ignorance, this is the contrast the passage is building. Ibn Kathir: Allah *knows the Unseen in its entirety;* He knows what His creatures do openly and what they do secretly, what is visible and what is concealed, what is secret and hidden — *"and He will requite them for that, for both minor and major actions."*

**"And I know not, perhaps it may be a trial for you, and an enjoyment for a while"** (111). Ibn Jarīr explained it: *'perhaps that is being delayed for you as a test for you, and enjoyment for an allotted time'* — a meaning narrated by ʿAwn from Ibn ʿAbbās. So on this reading the thing they are enjoying is a delay: **fitnah**, a trial or testing, and **matāʿ ilā hīn**, enjoyment up to an allotted time. Ibn Kathir closes the point as the scholars do when a meaning is reported rather than certain: *and Allah knows best.*

## The last words of the sūrah: a prayer (112)

*"My Lord! Judge in truth."* Ibn Kathir: *judge between us and our people who disbelieve in the truth.* Qatādah observed that **the Prophets (peace be upon them) used to say**, *"Our Lord! Judge between us and our people in truth, for You are the Best of those who give judgment"* (7:89) — and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to say this too. So the sūrah that has walked through prophet after prophet ends by putting their common prayer on his lips: he is one of that line, and the argument goes to the same Judge.

It was reported from Mālik, from Zayd bin Aslam, that **when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ witnessed any fighting, he would say: *"My Lord! Judge in truth."***

Then the closing clause, and it is the most beautiful turn in the passage: *"and our Lord is **ar-Rahmān**, the Most Gracious, Whose help is to be sought against that which you attribute."* The name invoked at the moment of confrontation is the name of mercy — the same theme as ayah 107, now as a name of Allah. Ibn Kathir explains *"that which you attribute"* as *'the various lies and fabrications that you utter, some of which are worse than others; Allah is the One Whose Help we seek against that.'*

So the sūrah ends where it must: the Messenger sent as a mercy, facing rejection, seeks help from ar-Rahmān. With this, Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ — *"To Allah be praise and blessings."*

## Living it

- **Ayah 106 makes the message plain and sufficient, and names who receives it — *ʿābidīn*, a people who worship.** By Ibn Kathir's definition that means worshipping Allah in the manner He has prescribed, loves and is pleased with, preferring His obedience to the Shaytān and one's own desires.
- **Take your model of firmness from ayah 109 and your model of temperament from ayah 107.** Clarity about what you believe and where you differ, declared openly so both sides know where they stand — and, as Muslim reports, he ﷺ refused to invoke a curse even when he was asked to: *"I was not sent as a curse, rather I was sent as a mercy."*
- **Do not read ease as safety** (111). On Ibn Jarīr's explanation, a delay may be a test and enjoyment for an allotted time.
- **When wronged, ask for truth** (112) — *"My Lord, judge in truth"* — and seek help in the name ar-Rahmān, the very name the ayah chooses at the moment of confrontation.
